question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — FAA, UNITED STATES
Governing provision: 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1) (private pilot privileges and limitations; BasicMed operations). BasicMed itself is established by 14 CFR part 68 and by section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016 (Pub. L. 114-190); the aircraft limits a BasicMed pilot must observe are written into § 61.113(i)(1).

Verbatim regulatory text (source of all three answers):
"(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and"
— 14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1), eCFR current text, fetched 2026-11-16T01:15:04Z (sha256 de6b7248669d), https://ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-61/subpart-E/section-61.113

1. MAXIMUM TAKEOFF WEIGHT — 12,500 pounds
   Limit: the aircraft's maximum takeoff weight must be not more than 12,500 lb. 12,500 lb is the ceiling and is itself permitted (the rule reads "not more than," an inclusive bound). "Maximum takeoff weight" here means the maximum certificated/approved takeoff weight of the aircraft as a design and certification figure, not the actual computed weight of a particular load — the actual takeoff weight on any flight must of course also be within that maximum per the aircraft's approved limitations.
   Practical test: if the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight exceeds 12,500 lb, it is not eligible for BasicMed operation, regardless of how light it is actually loaded on the day.

2. NUMBER OF OCCUPANTS THE AIRCRAFT MAY BE AUTHORIZED TO CARRY — 7 occupants
   Limit: the aircraft must be "authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants." This is a property of the aircraft — its certificated/placarded seating or occupant capacity (e.g., number of approved seats or the occupant count in its approved limitations) — not the number of people actually aboard on a given flight. An aircraft authorized for 8 or more occupants is excluded from BasicMed operation even if only two people fly in it.
   The pilot in command is an occupant. The 7-occupant figure includes the pilot.

3. NUMBER OF PASSENGERS ON BOARD — 6 passengers
   Limit: the flight must be "operated with no more than 6 passengers on board." Passengers means persons on board other than the pilot. This is a per-flight operational limit, distinct from the certification figure in item 2.
   Arithmetic consistency with item 2: occupants = pilot + passengers. With 1 pilot and 6 passengers, occupants = 7, which exactly equals (does not exceed) the 7-occupant authorization ceiling. The two numbers are the same limit expressed from two directions, and they agree.

HOW THE TWO OCCUPANCY LIMITS INTERACT (both must be satisfied):
   The binding passenger count is the lower of (a) 6 and (b) the aircraft's authorized occupant capacity minus the pilot. Examples:
   - Aircraft authorized for 7 occupants: max 6 passengers. Both limits bind at the same point.
   - Aircraft authorized for 4 occupants: max 3 passengers (4 − 1 pilot), even though the rule's numeric passenger cap is 6. The aircraft's own authorization is the tighter constraint.
   - Aircraft authorized for 8 occupants: not eligible at all under BasicMed (fails item 2).

FOURTH CONDITION IN THE SAME SENTENCE (stated so the list is not mistaken for the complete set of aircraft conditions):
   The aircraft must not be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29. A part 29 transport category rotorcraft fails § 61.113(i)(1) irrespective of weight, occupant count, or passenger count.

SCOPE AND CAVEATS:
   - Jurisdiction: United States, FAA rules only. These aircraft limits have no application outside US regulatory jurisdiction; a BasicMed pilot also faces separate operating limits in § 61.113(i) (for example on altitude, airspeed, and operations outside the United States) that are not part of the three questions asked and are not restated here as specifications.
   - The three figures above are aircraft/flight limits only. They say nothing about whether a given pilot is eligible to act under BasicMed; pilot eligibility (medical education course, physician examination, self-assessment, and the § 68.9 conditions) is a separate determination.
   - Currency: answer reflects the eCFR text of § 61.113 as fetched 2026-11-16. The figures are regulatory and can be amended; re-verify against the current eCFR text before relying on this for an operational or training document.

BOTTOM LINE: Under BasicMed a pilot may fly an aircraft with a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants (pilot included), carrying no more than 6 passengers on board, and not a part 29 transport category rotorcraft.

question: M3
answer:
HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS FOR A DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING COMMERCIAL MOTOR VEHICLE (MOTORCOACH), INTERSTATE US OPERATION

Governing authority: 49 CFR Part 395, Subpart A — specifically 49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles,' as applied by FMCSA's passenger-carrier hours-of-service guidance. Scope assumption stated up front: the driver operates a passenger-carrying CMV in interstate commerce, so the federal rule controls. If the operation is genuinely intrastate-only, a state's intrastate rule may differ and must be checked separately (see 'Scope limits' below).

1. THE THREE ANSWERS

(1) Maximum driving time: 10 hours. A driver may not drive more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1).

(2) Required consecutive off-duty period: 8 hours. Both daily limits in 395.5(a) are measured from '8 consecutive hours off duty.' The 8 hours must be consecutive and must be off duty (not merely on-duty-not-driving). 49 CFR 395.5(a).

(3) On-duty cutoff for driving: 15 hours. A driver may not drive for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty. 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2).

2. HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT (OPERATING RULE)

- The 10-hour and 15-hour limits are two independent ceilings that both must be satisfied. Whichever is reached first ends driving for that duty period.
- The 15-hour period is consecutive clock time starting when the driver comes on duty after the 8-hour off-duty reset. Breaks do not pause it, and on-duty-not-driving time (loading, inspections, paperwork, waiting while on duty) consumes the 15-hour window even though it does not consume the 10-hour driving allowance.
- Off-duty time does not count against either limit. To start a fresh 10/15 cycle the driver must take 8 consecutive hours off duty.
- Practical statement for a dispatcher: driving must be completed within 15 consecutive hours of coming on duty, and within that window no more than 10 of those hours may be driving.

Worked example: driver comes on duty at 06:00. Driving must stop no later than 21:00 (15 hours on duty), and the driver may log at most 10 hours of driving time inside 06:00–21:00. If the driver goes off duty at 21:00 and takes 8 consecutive hours off duty (21:00–05:00), a new cycle may begin at 05:00.

3. SECONDARY CUMULATIVE LIMITS (CONTEXT — NOT ANSWERS TO THE THREE ASKS)

The same regulation imposes cumulative on-duty ceilings that can bar driving even when the daily 10-hour and 15-hour limits are satisfied, 49 CFR 395.5(b):
- 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days, if the employing motor carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week; or
- 70 hours on duty in any period of 8 consecutive days, if the employing motor carrier operates CMVs every day of the week.
These are computed on total on duty time (driving plus on-duty-not-driving), across all motor carriers using the driver's services.
Note on restart: § 395.5 contains no 34-hour restart provision. The 34-hour restart in § 395.3(c) is written for property-carrying CMVs. A passenger-carrier operation should not assume a restart resets the 60/70-hour count without confirming the current rule text and any applicable exemption.

4. EXCEPTIONS AND EXEMPTIONS — OUT OF SCOPE, BUT MUST BE CHECKED BEFORE RELYING ON THE FIGURES

Section 395.5 is expressly '[s]ubject to the exceptions and exemptions in § 395.1.' The figures above are the standard limits and assume no exception applies. Before operational use, confirm whether any of the following applies to the specific operation: short-haul operations (§ 395.1(e)); adverse driving conditions (§ 395.1(b)); the 16-hour extension for certain short-haul drivers; driver-salesperson or other vocational exceptions; emergency relief (§ 390.23); state/local government or other statutory exemptions; and any Alaska/Hawaii provisions. Also confirm record-of-duty-status and ELD obligations (49 CFR 395.8 and 395.9) and their exceptions for the operation, since compliance evidence is separate from the limits themselves.
Sleeper-berth note: the split sleeper-berth provision in § 395.1(g) is written around property-carrying CMV drivers. This answer does not assert that a split sleeper-berth equivalent applies to a passenger-carrying driver, and does not use it to extend the 10- or 15-hour figures. If the operation wants to rely on a split, the current text of § 395.1(g) and FMCSA passenger-carrier guidance must be confirmed first.

5. SCOPE LIMITS AND CAVEATS

- Jurisdiction: federal interstate rule only. Intrastate-only passenger operations are governed by state rules, which in many states track the federal limits but are not uniform; no state figure is stated here because no state was identified.
- Currency: reflects the current codified text of 49 CFR 395.5 as of the source fetch (2026-11-16). The passenger-carrier limits in 395.5(a) were not changed by the 2020 property-carrier hours-of-service final rule, which amended the property-carrying provisions in 395.3 and related definitions.
- Historical versions are not addressed; only the current rule is stated.
- This is a regulatory summary, not legal advice; a carrier should confirm against the current eCFR text and any applicable exemption before relying on it in an enforcement context.

6. SOURCE VERIFICATION FOR EACH STATED VALUE

- 10 hours driving ← 395.5(a)(1): 'More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty' (prohibited), therefore the maximum permitted is 10. Verified against eCFR § 395.5 text and FMCSA passenger-carrier summary page.
- 8 consecutive hours off duty ← 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2): both limits run 'following 8 consecutive hours off duty.' Verified.
- 15 hours on duty ← 395.5(a)(2): 'For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty' (driving prohibited), therefore driving ends at 15 hours on duty. Verified.
- 60 hours/7 days and 70 hours/8 days ← 395.5(b)(1) and (b)(2). Verified; presented as context only.

question: M5
answer:
BOTTOM LINE
- Ask 1: 9 consecutive hours of scheduled rest.
- Ask 2: that rest may be reduced to 8 consecutive hours, but only if the flight attendant is given a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours that is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest.

1. GOVERNING RULE
14 CFR 135.273, 'Flight attendant duty period limitations and rest requirements,' in Part 135 Subpart F. Section 135.261 makes Subpart F (through 135.273) the flight-time, duty-period and rest rule set for operations conducted under Part 135, and 135.273 is the only FAA provision that sets a rest minimum specifically for flight attendants. It applies to flight attendants in all operations conducted under Part 135, including on-demand charter; the on-demand character of the flight does not remove the requirement.

135.273(b)(2):
"(2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

135.273(b)(3):
"(3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

2. THE FOUR CONDITIONS ON THE REDUCTION - ALL MUST BE MET
(a) The reduced rest must still be at least 8 consecutive hours. Eight is the floor; there is no further reduction, no splitting, and no adding of separate blocks to reach it.
(b) A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours must be provided.
(c) That 10-hour rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced (8-hour) rest. The anchor runs from the start of the reduced rest, not its end.
(d) Both rests must fall between duty periods (from completion of a scheduled duty period to commencement of the subsequent duty period), and both must be scheduled in advance. The rule speaks of a 'scheduled rest period,' so an 8-hour night created after the fact by an operational delay is not a compliant reduction.
If any condition fails, the 9-hour minimum governs and the 8-hour rest is a violation. The reduction is the certificate holder's scheduling election, not an entitlement the flight attendant may invoke.

3. WHAT COUNTS AS REST
- Rest means freedom from all duty; the attendant must be relieved of all duties for the full consecutive block.
- Transportation that is not local in character and that the certificate holder requires and provides is not counted as part of the rest period (practitioner expectation consistent with the rule's structure; confirm the operator's GOM wording). A company-arranged long repositioning leg or van transfer cannot be parked inside the 8 or 9 hours.
- The rest must be consecutive, not two blocks that sum to 9.

4. OPERATOR PROCEDURE (COMPLIANCE CONTROL)
Step 1 - Schedule check: for every pairing carrying a flight attendant, compute scheduled duty end to next duty start. If the scheduled duty period is 14 hours or less, block at least 9 consecutive hours of rest between the duty periods. Recommended practice: plan 10 hours so a delay does not by itself create a violation.
Step 2 - If using the reduction: build the 8-hour rest and the following 10-hour-or-more rest into the same trip sheet, verify that the 10-hour rest starts no later than 24 hours after the start of the 8-hour rest, and annotate the pairing with the reduction reference so the two-rest transaction is visible on audit.
Step 3 - Day of operations: any delay that would shrink a 9-hour rest below 9, shrink an 8-hour rest below 8, or push the start of the 10-hour compensatory rest past the 24-hour anchor is a non-compliance event requiring re-planning (delay the next duty period), not a note in the file.
Step 4 - Records: retain scheduled and actual duty and rest times in the duty-time records kept under 135.63 and in trip paperwork, so the 9/8+10 structure is auditable.
Step 5 - Escalation: if the 10-hour compensatory rest cannot be guaranteed at the time the 8-hour rest is scheduled, do not schedule the reduction; use 9 hours.

5. WORKED EXAMPLE
Scheduled duty Day 1: 06:00-20:00 (14 h 00 m); attendant released at 20:30 after post-flight duties.
- Baseline: rest 20:30 Day 1 to 05:30 Day 2 = 9 h 00 m. Compliant.
- Reduction: rest 20:30 Day 1 to 04:30 Day 2 = 8 h 00 m. This requires a subsequent rest of at least 10 consecutive hours beginning no later than 20:30 Day 2 (24 hours after 20:30 Day 1). If Day 2 duty is 05:00-15:00, the subsequent rest begins 15:00 Day 2 - inside the anchor - and must run to at least 01:00 Day 3. Compliant.
- Non-compliant variant: if Day 2 duty ran 05:00-21:00, the subsequent rest would begin 21:00 Day 2, after the 20:30 anchor. The 8-hour reduction is then unavailable and the Day 1 rest had to be a full 9 hours.

6. SCOPE LIMITS OF THIS ANSWER
- This is the FAA regulatory floor. The operator's approved manuals or operations specifications, or a collective bargaining agreement, may impose more (10 hours is common); the more restrictive requirement applies. No operator-specific operations specification or manual provision was available for review, so none is asserted here; the figures above change only if the operator's approved documents are stricter - they cannot be less strict.
- Duty periods longer than 14 hours are governed by other provisions of 135.273 and are outside this answer.
- If the individual also acts as a required flight crewmember during the same operation, the flight-crewmember duty and rest rules of 135.263 through 135.267 apply to that person in that capacity and the more restrictive requirement governs; those figures are not stated here.
- If a given flight is actually conducted under Part 121 or Part 125 (dual-certificate holder), that part's rules govern that flight rather than 135.273.
- State or foreign law is not addressed and may add requirements on top of the FAA minimum.

question: M7
answer:
## Answer

As of the RFC Editor / IETF Datatracker records consulted (fetched 2026-11-16T01:18:57Z per the research facts):

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| 1. Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2* (IETF Standards Track, June 2022) |
| 2. RFCs directly obsoleted by RFC 9113 | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

### Detail for Ask 1

**RFC 9113, HTTP/2**, is the current base specification of HTTP/2. It is a Standards Track RFC published in June 2022. Extensions and companion documents that reference HTTP/2 are not the base specification, and errata against RFC 9113 do not change the RFC number that specifies HTTP/2.

Authoritative locations:

- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113

### Detail for Ask 2

RFC 9113 directly obsoletes:

1. **RFC 7540** — *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)*, May 2015.
2. **RFC 8740** — *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*, February 2020.

Basis: the RFC 9113 document states: 'This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740.' The RFC Editor defines 'Obsoletes' as the RFCs that the newer document completely replaces; it is the direct obsolescence relation named in the current RFC, not the entire historical chain and not an 'Updates' relationship.

For avoidance of doubt: RFC 7541 (HPACK) is not in RFC 9113's Obsoletes list and is therefore not part of this answer.

### Verification procedure

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html or https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113.
2. Confirm the title is *HTTP/2* and the category is Standards Track.
3. Read the document's **Obsoletes** field; it must read **7540, 8740**.
4. Check https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113 for status and errata. Errata, if any, clarify the text but do not change which RFC is the specification or the Obsoletes list.
5. Do not include documents related by **Updates** rather than **Obsoletes**, and do not expand to a historical chain unless an earlier RFC is itself separately named in the current RFC's Obsoletes field.
6. If a later RFC appears in RFC 9113's 'Obsoleted by' status field, that later RFC would become the current specification and this lookup must be rerun.

### Scope note

'Current' here means the latest published Standards Track RFC that is the base HTTP/2 specification, determined from RFC Editor / IETF publication records, not from drafts, errata, or extension documents.

question: M9
answer:
## UK statutory minimum wage rates from April 2026

| Statutory rate | Age band | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---:|---:|
| National Living Wage (NLW) | 21 and over | **£12.71** |
| National Minimum Wage (NMW) 18-20 Year Old Rate | 18 or over but not yet 21 | **£10.85** |

**Answers**

1. **National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over from April 2026: £12.71 per hour.**
2. **National Minimum Wage for 18 to 20 year olds: £10.85 per hour.**

### Application notes for HR/payroll

- These are the **gross statutory hourly rates** published by GOV.UK for the rates effective from **1 April 2026**. The governing instrument is the **National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026**, which come into force on 1 April 2026.
- For payroll, apply the rates from the first pay reference period beginning on or after 1 April 2026, in line with the NMW pay reference period rules.
- The 18-20 figure is the **standard 18-20 Year Old Rate**, not the apprentice rate. For completeness, the same April 2026 schedule lists: 16-17 Year Old Rate **£8.00**, Apprentice Rate **£8.00**, and Accommodation Offset **£11.10**.
- Workers aged 21 and over are entitled to the NLW rate of **£12.71**; workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21 are entitled to the 18-20 rate of **£10.85**.
- The London Living Wage is a separate voluntary rate and is not the statutory National Living Wage.

**Sources:** GOV.UK, *National Minimum Wage rates*; GOV.UK, *The National Minimum Wage in 2026*; GOV.UK, *Minimum wage rates for 2026*; GOV.UK news release, *National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour*; National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026.
cautions: The answer gives 12.71 GBP per hour for ask 1, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION — RODS RELIEF DETERMINATION

Assumed scope: property-carrying commercial motor vehicle operation under FMCSA jurisdiction, current 49 CFR Part 395. Regulatory basis: 49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1), current eCFR text.

1. ANSWERS
1.1 Radius — 150 air miles. The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation states the equivalent as 172.6 statute miles. This is a straight-line air-mile radius, not a road-mile radius.
1.2 Release — 14 consecutive hours. The driver must return to the normal work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14-hour window is continuous and runs from the driver coming on duty; it is not a 14-hour driving limit and is not paused by breaks.

2. QUOTED REGULATORY TEXT
49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1): '(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if: (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location; (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours; ...'

3. EFFECT OF THE EXCEPTION
When every condition of § 395.1(e)(1) is met, the driver is exempt from the records-of-duty-status requirements of § 395.8 and the supporting-document requirements of § 395.11. The exemption is conditional, not a blanket relief from Part 395. If the driver operates outside the 150 air-mile radius or is not returned to the normal work reporting location and released from work within 14 consecutive hours, the exemption does not apply for that operation and the driver must comply with § 395.8 RODS requirements.

4. MEASUREMENT AND COMPLIANCE PROCEDURE
Step 1 — Fix the normal work reporting location. Use the location where the driver normally reports for work; do not substitute a terminal, dispatch office, or customer site unless that is genuinely the normal reporting location.
Step 2 — Measure the radius in air miles. Measure straight-line distance from the normal work reporting location to every point the driver operates. The maximum is 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles). Road distance is not the test.
Step 3 — Establish the 14-hour clock. Record the time the driver comes on duty. The driver must return to the normal work reporting location and be released from work by the end of the 14th consecutive hour. Breaks, meals, and waiting time do not extend the 14-hour window.
Step 4 — Verify all other § 395.1(e)(1) conditions. The two values above are the thresholds asked about, not the complete eligibility checklist. The remaining conditions of § 395.1(e)(1) must also be satisfied. If any condition fails, the RODS exemption is unavailable.
Step 5 — Document and monitor. Retain dispatch, GPS or geofence, time-clock, or equivalent records sufficient to show the driver stayed within 150 air miles and was returned and released within 14 consecutive hours. Re-evaluate whenever routes, reporting locations, or schedules change.

5. SPECIAL NOTE ON DRIVER-SALESPERSON
Clause (ii) expressly carves out a driver-salesperson from the return/release language. If the driver is a driver-salesperson, do not apply the 14-hour return/release condition mechanically; check the separate treatment of driver-salespersons under Part 395.

6. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID
- Using 100 air miles or 12 hours, which are the superseded short-haul values.
- Using road miles instead of air miles.
- Treating the 14-hour limit as a driving-time limit only.
- Assuming the exception is automatic rather than conditional on all § 395.1(e)(1) criteria.

7. RESULT TABLE
Ask 1 — Radius: 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles).
Ask 2 — Release: 14 consecutive hours.

8. BOTTOM LINE
For the FMCSA short-haul exception in § 395.1(e)(1), the driver must operate within 150 air miles of the normal work reporting location and must return to that location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — REGULATORY ANSWER

CONTROLLING AUTHORITY
14 CFR 61.113(i)(1) (current eCFR text), read with the FAA's current BasicMed program page. Operative text:

  '(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and'

FAA BasicMed page (current): 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants' / 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds.'

THE THREE LIMITS

1) Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 pounds.
   - Meaning: the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) per its type certificate / AFM, not the actual weight at which the flight is conducted. A flight at 4,800 lb actual in an aircraft certificated to 14,000 lb MTOW is NOT BasicMed-eligible; the certification basis is what is tested.
   - The regulation's phrase is 'maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds'; FAA guidance phrases it 'maximum certificated takeoff weight.' Same quantity. 12,500 lb is inclusive (not more than = 12,500 is permitted).

2) Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 occupants.
   - Meaning: the aircraft's certificated/authorized maximum occupancy under federal law (seating capacity, placards, type certificate data sheet, AFM limitations), including required flight crew members. It is a property of the aircraft's authorization, not a count of who is actually aboard on a given flight.
   - 7 is inclusive: an aircraft authorized for exactly 7 occupants is eligible; one authorized for 8 is not.

3) Passengers on board: 6 passengers.
   - Meaning: an operational limit on the flight — no more than 6 passengers may actually be carried. 'Passengers' = occupants other than required flight crew. This is consistent with limit (2): 7 authorized occupants minus 1 required pilot = 6 passengers. An aircraft authorized for 7 occupants flown single-pilot may carry 6 passengers; if the flight requires two crew, only 5 passengers may be aboard, because the occupant ceiling of 7 still binds.

ADDITIONAL AIRCRAFT-ELIGIBILITY CONDITION IN THE SAME SENTENCE (not one of the three asks, but part of the same test)
The aircraft must not be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under 14 CFR part 29. A part 29 transport-category helicopter therefore fails BasicMed eligibility regardless of weight or seating.

CURRENCY / VERSION WARNING — READ BEFORE CITING ANY OTHER SOURCE
These limits were expanded by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 and reflected in the current 61.113(i)(1). Material predating that expansion still shows the OLD limits:
   - superseded: 6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight
   - superseded: not more than 6 occupants
   - superseded: no more than 5 passengers on board
FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A (2017) still contains the old figures ('maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs'; 'up to six occupants ... up to five passengers on board'). Do not use AC 68-1A, the 2017 BasicMed articles, or any cached guidance for the current numbers. Verify against eCFR 61.113(i) or the FAA BasicMed page before relying on this answer.
The figures above reflect the rule as published at the time of writing (eCFR 'current' retrieved 2026-11-16). Because BasicMed limits have changed once already, a flight conducted on a different date should be checked against the rule in force on that date.

DISTINCTIONS THE QUESTION CAN CONFLATE
- Occupants vs. passengers: occupants = everyone aboard including required crew; passengers = occupants minus required crew. The rule caps both, and the occupant cap governs the aircraft's authorization while the passenger cap governs the flight.
- Certificated vs. actual weight: the 12,500 lb test is on the certificate, not the scale.
- These are aircraft-eligibility limits. They are separate from the other BasicMed operating conditions — the 18,000 ft MSL altitude ceiling, the 250-knot indicated-airspeed limit, and the no-compensation/no-hire restriction for carriage of passengers or property — and from the pilot-side requirements (valid U.S. driver's license, medical education course, comprehensive medical examination, self-assessment before each flight). An aircraft meeting 12,500 lb / 7 occupants / 6 passengers is still not BasicMed-legal if the flight violates those operating conditions.

HOW TO APPLY (verification procedure)
1. Pull the aircraft's type certificate data sheet and AFM Limitations section. Record (a) maximum certificated takeoff weight and (b) maximum authorized occupancy/seating capacity.
2. If MTOW > 12,500 lb, or authorized occupancy > 7, the pilot may not act as PIC under BasicMed in that aircraft — a medical certificate (or a different operating authority) is required.
3. If the aircraft is a transport category rotorcraft certified under part 29, it is ineligible regardless of 1 and 2.
4. Plan the flight so that persons aboard other than required crew do not exceed 6.
5. Confirm the pilot-side BasicMed qualifications and the altitude/speed/compensation conditions separately.

SUMMARY OF VALUES: maximum takeoff weight 12,500 pounds; occupants authorized 7; passengers on board 6.

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of Service — Driver of a Passenger-Carrying Commercial Motor Vehicle (US, Federal)

**Governing rule:** 49 CFR § 395.5, *Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles* (FMCSA). This is the passenger-carrying rule. It is **not** § 395.3, which governs property-carrying CMVs and uses different numbers.

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** of driving, following 8 consecutive hours off duty |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours off duty** — this is the off-duty interval that must precede the driving period and starts a fresh cycle |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours on duty** following those 8 consecutive hours off duty |

All three are stated in the regulation itself; none is derived or computed.

## 2. Regulatory text (quoted)

49 CFR § 395.5(a):

> "(a) No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Related weekly ceilings in the same section, § 395.5(b) — **context only, not part of the three answers**:

> "(b) ... for any period after—
> (1) Having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
> (2) Having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week."

## 3. How the three limits interlock (operational reading)

- The **8 consecutive hours off duty** is the trigger. When the driver completes 8 consecutive hours off duty, a new cycle begins: the driver has a fresh 10-hour driving allowance and a fresh 15-hour on-duty window.
- The **15-hour on-duty window** runs from the moment the driver comes on duty after that 8-hour break. Driving is prohibited for any period after the 15th hour on duty, regardless of how much of the 10-hour driving allowance remains unused.
- The **10 driving hours need not be consecutive** and may be split across the window, but every driving hour must fall inside the 15-hour window, and no driving may occur after hour 15.
- Non-driving on-duty work (loading, paperwork, inspections, dispatch) consumes the 15-hour window but not the 10-hour driving allowance.
- **Worked example:** driver completes 8 consecutive hours off duty and comes on duty at 06:00. The 15-hour window closes at 21:00. The driver may drive up to 10 hours total between 06:00 and 21:00; at 21:00 the driver must be off the wheel even if only, say, 7 driving hours were used. Five hours of the window remain available for non-driving on-duty work.

## 4. What does **not** apply (guards against the standard error)

The following are **property-carrying** limits under § 395.3 and must not be substituted for the passenger answers above:

- 11 hours maximum driving (property) — **not applicable**; passenger limit is 10.
- 14-hour on-duty window (property) — **not applicable**; passenger window is 15.
- 10 consecutive hours off duty (property) — **not applicable**; passenger requirement is 8 consecutive hours.
- 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours (property, § 395.3(a)(3)(ii)) — **no equivalent break requirement is imposed on passenger-carrying drivers by § 395.5**. Carrier policy or state law may still require breaks.
- The 34-hour restart in § 395.3(c) is written for property-carrying operations; § 395.5 contains no restart provision, and the 60/70-hour ceilings are computed over the rolling 7- or 8-day period.
- The split sleeper-berth provision in § 395.1(g) is written for property-carrying CMV drivers; for a passenger-carrying driver the 8-hour off-duty period must be **consecutive** and is not split. Confirm against § 395.1(g) for the specific operation before relying on this.

## 5. Scope conditions attached to these answers

These three values are correct **as stated** for a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV operating in interstate commerce under federal jurisdiction, with no applicable exemption. Before applying them to a specific operation, confirm:

1. **Vehicle class.** § 395.5 applies to a "passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle" as defined in 49 CFR § 390.5 (broadly, a vehicle designed or used to transport more than 8 passengers including the driver for compensation, or more than 15 passengers including the driver not for compensation). A motorcoach qualifies.
2. **Interstate status.** Federal rules apply to interstate operations. Transporting passengers entirely within one state can still be interstate commerce if the passengers began or will conclude their trip outside the state (FMCSA passenger-carrier guidance). Purely intrastate operations may fall under a state HOS rule instead — several states adopt the federal standard, some do not, and a state rule may be stricter.
3. **Exemptions.** 49 CFR § 395.1 contains exemptions and modifications (e.g., certain school bus, government, and limited/short-haul operations). None should be assumed to apply to a general motorcoach operation without specific facts.
4. **Adverse driving conditions.** § 395.1(b) provides limited relief when a driver encounters adverse driving conditions that could not reasonably have been known. Where it applies to a passenger-carrying driver it may extend the driving time, but it does not extend the 15-hour on-duty period. Treat this as an exception to be documented at the time, not as a routine allowance; the three core answers above remain the baseline.
5. **Weekly ceilings still bind.** A driver who is fully compliant with 10/8/15 can still be prohibited from driving by the § 395.5(b) 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day ceiling.
6. **Recordkeeping.** Drivers subject to § 395.5 must keep records of duty status (ELD or paper RODS as permitted under Part 395 Subpart B); the limits above are enforced through those records and through carrier scheduling obligations, which are imposed on the motor carrier as well as the driver ("No motor carrier shall permit or require...").
7. **Currency of the rule.** The quoted text is the current effective text of 49 CFR § 395.5. Re-verify against eCFR before relying on this in an enforcement or audit setting, since HOS rules are amended periodically.

## 6. One-line answer

A driver of a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle in the US may drive **10 hours** following **8 consecutive hours off duty**, and may not drive for any period after having been **on duty 15 hours** following those 8 consecutive hours off duty (49 CFR § 395.5(a)).

question: M5
answer:
COMPLIANCE ANSWER — 14 CFR Part 135 flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less

1. DIRECT ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Required rest. A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours.
Authority: 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(2), Part 135 Subpart F. Quoted text: "(2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours."

Ask 2 — Permitted reduction. That 9-hour rest period may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours — and no lower. The reduction is conditional, not automatic.
Authority: 14 CFR § 135.273(b)(3). Quoted text: "(3) The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period."

Bottom line: 9 consecutive hours required; 8 consecutive hours is the floor; the 1-hour reduction is available only when the 10-consecutive-hour subsequent rest is actually scheduled inside the 24-hour window.

2. CONDITIONS ATTACHED TO THE REDUCTION (all must be satisfied)

A. The attendant is in fact provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. Not "planned for later" — scheduled.
B. That subsequent rest period is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced (8-hour) rest period.
C. That subsequent rest period occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
D. If any condition in A–C fails, the reduction is unavailable and the full 9 consecutive hours must be given. There is no intermediate value between 8 and 9 and no floor below 8 anywhere in Part 135 for flight attendants.

Derived scheduling constraint (arithmetic, not regulatory text): 24 hours − 8 hours reduced rest = 16 hours. The subsequent 10-hour rest must begin within 16 hours of the end of the reduced rest. Because a scheduled duty period under (b)(1)/(b)(2) is capped at 14 hours, the 16-hour window is normally not the binding constraint; it becomes binding when report-to-release, deadhead, or ground time between the two rests runs long.

3. WORKED EXAMPLE

Scheduled duty period: 06:00–20:00 (14.0 hours — at the limit, still "14 hours or less").
- Standard compliance: rest 20:00 to 05:00 next day (9 consecutive hours). No further condition attaches.
- Reduced-rest option: rest 20:00 to 04:00 (8 consecutive hours). Reduced rest began at 20:00, so the subsequent 10-hour rest must begin no later than 20:00 the following day. If the next duty period runs 04:00–18:00, the subsequent rest can start at 18:00 — inside the window (18:00 < 20:00), condition satisfied. If that duty period instead releases at 20:30, the 10-hour rest cannot begin within 24 hours of 20:00 and the reduction was invalid from the start; the full 9 hours should have been scheduled.

4. APPLICABILITY AND SCOPE (state these to the client alongside the numbers)

- Who the rule binds: § 135.273 governs certificate holders operating under Part 135 who use flight attendants. The flight-attendant crew requirement itself comes from § 135.107: "No certificate holder may operate an aircraft that has a passenger seating configuration, excluding any pilot seat, of more than 19 unless there is a flight attendant crewmember on board the aircraft." For aircraft at 19 or fewer passenger seats, § 135.107 alone does not mandate a flight attendant; the rest rule applies when the operator carries one. Confirm the operator's seating configuration before treating § 135.273 as triggered on a given airframe.
- Duty period over 14 hours: outside this answer. The 9/8 answer is expressly limited to a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less; do not extend it.
- Stricter overlays: a collective bargaining agreement, operations manual, OpSpec, or company policy may impose more than 9 hours or forbid the reduction. The regulatory figures are floors on rest, not ceilings — a stricter contract term controls the schedule.
- Correct citation: § 135.273, not § 135.267. § 135.267 is the flight time/duty limitation rule for crewmembers generally and is not the flight attendant rest provision.

5. RECORDKEEPING / IMPLEMENTATION PROCEDURE

For each pairing that uses the 8-hour reduction, the scheduling record should show, at minimum: (a) the preceding scheduled duty period's report and release times; (b) the reduced rest start and end times; (c) the subsequent 10-hour rest start and end times; (d) confirmation that (c) began within 24 hours of (b) beginning. Retain with the duty/flight time records the operator keeps under Part 135 (see § 135.63; confirm the specific paragraph against the current rule text and the operator's approved manual before finalizing the record form). Flag reduced-rest pairings in the scheduling system so the 10-hour leg cannot be silently dropped by a later schedule change.

6. VERIFICATION NOTE

Both quoted passages were retrieved from the eCFR Subpart F / § 135.273 pages during this project and are reproduced verbatim above; the answers rest on those quotes rather than on paraphrase. The text of § 135.273(b)(1) (the paragraph under which the 14-hour-or-less duty period is scheduled) and any further subsections of § 135.273 were not quoted in the retrieved material and should be read in full before the operator's manual language is finalized. That does not change the two values above, which are quoted directly from (b)(2) and (b)(3).

question: M7
answer:
# Current HTTP/2 specification and what it obsoletes

## Answer

| Ask | Answer |
|---|---|
| Current specification of HTTP/2 | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, Standards Track (Proposed Standard), June 2022 |
| RFCs it obsoletes | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (exactly two) |

Document identifiers:

- **RFC 9113** — *HTTP/2* (June 2022). IETF HTTPBIS working group; Standards Track, currently Proposed Standard. Part of the HTTP/2 revision set published alongside RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1) and RFC 9114 (HTTP/3).
- **RFC 7540** — *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* (May 2015). The original HTTP/2 core specification; now obsolete.
- **RFC 8740** — *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2* (February 2020). Obsoleted because its TLS 1.3 guidance was folded into RFC 9113.

## Evidence (primary source, quoted)

From the IETF Datatracker record for RFC 9113 (https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/):

- "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
- "This is an Internet Standards Track document."

These two statements supply both answers directly: the document identity (RFC 9113) and the complete obsoletes list (7540, 8740). No inference from secondary sources is required.

## Distinctions that matter for this answer

1. **"Obsoletes" vs. "Updates".** An RFC header can carry both an `Obsoletes:` and an `Updates:` line, and they mean different things. *Obsoletes* replaces a document outright; *updates* amends a document that remains in force. The two entries above come from the `Obsoletes:` designation only. Do not merge an `Updates:` list into the answer.
2. **RFC 9113 does not obsolete the whole HTTP/2 family.** These remain current and are *not* in the obsoletes list:
   - **RFC 7541** — *HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2* (still the current header-compression spec for HTTP/2).
   - **RFC 8441** — *Bootstrapping WebSockets with HTTP/2* (extended CONNECT).
   - **RFC 8336** — *The ORIGIN HTTP/2 Frame*.
   If the question is read as "the HTTP/2 core protocol specification," RFC 9113 alone is the answer; if it were read as "every document in the HTTP/2 suite," RFC 9113 would still be the only *core* spec, with the above as companions. The obsoletes answer does not change either way.
3. **Status.** RFC 9113 is Standards Track (Proposed Standard). RFC 7540 was also Standards Track (Proposed Standard); its obsolescence is a document-identity change, not a status change. Neither document has advanced to Internet Standard.
4. **Currency.** The answer is correct as of the source snapshot recorded in the research notes (Datatracker page for RFC 9113, fetched 2026-11-16T01:25:47Z). No HTTP/2 core successor to RFC 9113 was found in the gathered sources. If a future revision (e.g., an RFC 9113bis) is published, this answer changes to that number and the obsoletes list becomes "RFC 7540, RFC 8740, RFC 9113."

## Re-verification procedure (if currency must be re-established)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.txt and read the header block. Confirm the line `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740` and the status line `Proposed Standard`.
2. Open https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ and confirm the document status is not marked "Obsoleted" or "Replaced" and that no `Obsoleted by:` field is present.
3. Search the RFC Editor index for documents titled *HTTP/2* published after RFC 9113 (https://www.rfc-editor.org/search/rfc_search.php, title contains "HTTP/2", sorted by number descending). Any hit newer than 9113 whose header says `Obsoletes: 9113` supersedes this answer.
4. Cross-check the HTTPBIS working-group document list for an active `http2bis`-style draft; an active bis draft is the leading indicator that RFC 9113 will be superseded, though it does not change the answer until publication.
5. Check the errata page (https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/rfc9113) only for correctness of the text; errata do not change the obsoletes designation.

## Common wrong answers to avoid

- **"RFC 7540"** — this is the *obsolete* original, not the current spec. It is the answer to "what did RFC 9113 replace," not to "what is current."
- **"RFC 7541"** — HPACK, a companion document, never the core HTTP/2 specification and not obsoleted by RFC 9113.
- **"RFC 9113 obsoletes RFC 7541"** — incorrect; HPACK survives the revision.
- **Listing only RFC 7540** — incomplete; RFC 8740 is also formally obsoleted.

question: M9
answer:
UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES FROM APRIL 2026 — HR BRIEFING NOTE

1. THE TWO RATES REQUESTED

| Band | Statutory rate from April 2026 |
|---|---|
| National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | £12.71 per hour |
| National Minimum Wage — workers aged 18 to 20 | £10.85 per hour |

Both are confirmed, published statutory rates for the April 2026 uprating — not Low Pay Commission projections and not the voluntary Real Living Wage. Both are quoted to the penny, as statute requires, and both are gross hourly minima.

2. WHEN THEY TAKE EFFECT

The rates change on 1 April each year. The operative rule for payroll is that the new rates must be used from the first pay reference period that starts on or after 1 April 2026. A pay period that straddles 1 April (for example a weekly pay period running 30 March – 5 April 2026) is paid at the old rates; the first full period beginning on or after 1 April is paid at the new ones. Do not pro-rate across the boundary unless your payroll system already handles the change on that basis.

3. LEGAL BASIS AND BAND DEFINITIONS

The National Living Wage is the statutory minimum wage for workers aged 21 and over — it is not a separate voluntary scheme. The 21+ threshold has applied since April 2024 (it was 23+ before that); the band definitions in force for the April 2026 uprating are: 21 and over, 18 to 20, under 18, and apprentice. The two figures above are for the first two bands only.

Out of scope but noted for completeness so they are not confused with the answers: the under-18 rate and the apprentice rate are both £8.00 from April 2026, and a separate accommodation offset applies where an employer provides living accommodation. Different rules also apply to apprentices in their first year and to apprentices aged 21+ who are not in the first year of their apprenticeship. None of these are answers to the questions asked.

4. ILLUSTRATIVE SALARY CONVERSIONS (derived, not statutory)

These are arithmetic illustrations only, using 52 weeks:

| Band | 37.5 hrs/week | 40 hrs/week |
|---|---|---|
| 21+ NLW at £12.71 | £24,784.50 | £26,436.80 |
| 18–20 NMW at £10.85 | £21,157.50 | £22,568.00 |

Use the hourly statutory figure, not these annualised numbers, for any compliance calculation: paid overtime, overtime premia, salary sacrifice, deductions for uniforms or training, and unpaid working time can all pull effective pay below the hourly floor even where the headline annual salary looks adequate.

5. COMMON ERRORS TO AVOID

- Confusing the statutory NLW (£12.71) with the voluntary Real Living Wage, which is set independently by the Living Wage Foundation and is not a legal minimum.
- Assuming the 21+ rate applies to everyone; 18–20 year olds must be paid at least £10.85, and paying a 19-year-old £12.71 is permissible but paying them £11.00 because 'it's above the 18–20 rate' is only compliant if it is also above every applicable floor — check which band the worker actually falls in.
- Applying new rates from 1 April itself rather than from the first pay period starting on or after 1 April.
- Treating these as GB-only: the same statutory rates apply across the UK, including Northern Ireland. Devolved agricultural wage orders (for example in Scotland) can set higher floors for agricultural workers and should be checked separately where relevant.

6. SOURCES

- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' — https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates (rate table for April 2026: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8; apprentice £8; 'The rates change on 1 April every year.')
- GOV.UK, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' — https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026 ('The 18-20 Year Old Rate increases by 8.5 per cent in April to reach £10.85.')
