question: M11
answer:
# FMCSA Short-Haul Exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) — the two qualifying figures

## 1. Bottom line

| Ask | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Radius within which the driver must operate, measured from the normal work reporting location | **150 air-miles** |
| 2 | Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** (maximum duty period) |

Governing provision: **49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)**, current text, as amended by the FMCSA hours-of-service final rule published **June 1, 2020 (FR Doc. 2020-11469)**.

Operative regulatory language (current text):

> "A driver is exempt from the requirements of § 395.8 and § 395.11 if: the driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location, and the driver does not exceed a maximum duty period of 14 hours."
> — FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations*, current text of § 395.1(e)(1)

The 2020 rule preamble states the change expressly: the rule "extends the maximum duty period allowed under the short-haul exception in 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) from 12 hours to 14 hours" and "extends the maximum radius in which the short-haul exception applies from 100 to 150 air-miles."

## 2. Version control — make sure you are using the 2020 text

The correct pair today is **150 air-miles / 14 hours**.

**Superseded (pre-June 1, 2020): 100 air-miles / 12 hours.** Any visor card, dispatch rule, driver handbook, log-audit script or training slide still showing 100/12 is out of date and will wrongly disqualify compliant drivers (or wrongly qualify non-compliant ones). No conflicting current authority was found; the 100/12 pair is historical only.

## 3. How each figure is measured

### 3.1 The 150 air-mile radius

- **Measured from the normal work reporting location** — the location the carrier designates as the place the driver normally reports for duty. It is not the driver's residence, and it is not necessarily the terminal where the tractor is parked, although in most operations those coincide. For multi-terminal or remote-based drivers, the designation must be documented, because the whole radius is computed from it.
- **"Air-mile" means straight-line (great-circle) distance, not highway mileage.** A 170-road-mile out-and-back can sit inside 150 air-miles; a shorter but circuitous route can fall outside. Routes near the boundary must be checked geometrically, not by odometer.
- **It is a route condition, not a single-point condition.** Every point the driver serves during the work period must lie within 150 air-miles of the normal work reporting location.

### 3.2 The 14 consecutive hours

- **The clock starts when the driver comes on duty / reports for duty** at the beginning of the work period.
- **Two things must happen inside the 14 hours:** (a) the driver returns to the normal work reporting location, and (b) the driver is released from work.
- **The 14 hours run consecutively.** Off-duty time taken in the middle of the day — a meal break, a nap, waiting to be loaded — does **not** pause, stop or extend the 14-hour clock. A driver who takes a 2-hour off-duty break mid-shift must still be released by the 14th hour.
- **14 hours is an outer limit, not a target.** The 11-hour driving cap still binds inside it, so a driver cannot drive the full 14.

## 4. What the exception does and does not relieve

| Relieved for a qualifying driver | Not relieved |
|---|---|
| Records of duty status, § 395.8 | 11-hour driving limit |
| Supporting documents, § 395.11 | 10 consecutive hours off duty between duty periods |
| ELD requirement | 60/70-hour limits |
| 30-minute break (§ 395.1(e)(1)) — per FMCSA visor card: "Passenger and property carriers qualifying for the short-haul exception are not required to use a RODS or ELD, or take a 30-minute break" | All other Part 395 and vehicle/driver-safety requirements |

The exception is a **records** relief, not an hours-of-service relief. This is the single most common misreading.

## 5. The carrier-side condition that is routinely missed

The driver is excused from RODS, but the **motor carrier is not excused from recordkeeping**. The carrier must maintain and retain for six months accurate and true time records showing, for each day: the time the driver reports for duty, total hours on duty, the time the driver is released from duty, and the driver's total hours on duty for the preceding 7 days. Build this into the back office; a short-haul operation with no time records is out of compliance even when every driver qualifies.

## 6. Which drivers this covers

Post-2020, the 150 air-mile / 14 hour short-haul exception in § 395.1(e)(1) applies to **both property-carrying and passenger-carrying** CMV operations. The figures are the same for both classes under the current text; the old property/passenger divergence in the figures no longer exists at this paragraph.

## 7. Day-by-day application (how to operationalize it)

The exception is tested **per driver, per day**. If on any given day any qualifying condition fails — the driver goes outside 150 air-miles, is released after hour 14, or lacks the required off-duty time — the driver does **not** hold the exception for that day and must account for that day with RODS/ELD. Recommended dispatch test, run before releasing a driver to a route:

1. Is every stop on today's route within 150 straight-line air-miles of the designated normal work reporting location? (If no → RODS/ELD today.)
2. Will the driver be back at the reporting location and released from duty within 14 hours of coming on duty? (If no → RODS/ELD today.)
3. Does the driver have the required off-duty time before this duty period? (If no → RODS/ELD today.)
4. Is the carrier's six-month time record being generated for this driver-day? (If no → fix the back office regardless.)

## 8. Verify before relying on these points (not established by the sources used here)

- **Any "5 days in any 7" or "3 days in 7" usage cap.** Some secondary summaries describe such a limit on short-haul operations. I could not verify that against the current regulatory text with the sources available, so I am not asserting it either way. Read § 395.1(e) in full and confirm with FMCSA before encoding it as a hard rule.
- **The driver-salesperson carve-out** in the return-to-location / release-from-work language — confirm whether any driver in your fleet falls in that category.
- **Interaction with the adverse driving conditions exception (§ 395.1(b)(1))** — whether the 2-hour adverse-conditions extension can reach the short-haul 14-hour release condition. Confirm with FMCSA or counsel; do not assume.
- **State-specific requirements and Canada/Mexico operations** — this answer is FMCSA-only.
- **Designation of the normal work reporting location** for remote-based and multi-terminal drivers — document it in writing, per driver, because the entire 150 air-mile computation depends on it.

## 9. Sources

1. FMCSA, *Summary of Hours of Service Regulations* (current text of § 395.1(e)(1)) — https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/hours-service/summary-hours-service-regulations
2. FMCSA final rule, *Hours of Service of Drivers*, published June 1, 2020, FR Doc. 2020-11469 — https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2020/06/01/2020-11469
3. FMCSA, *Interstate Truck Driver's Guide to Hours of Service* (current edition) — https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/sites/fmcsa.dot.gov/files/2022-04/FMCSA-HOS-395-DRIVERS-GUIDE-TO-HOS(2022-04-28).pdf
4. FMCSA HOS Visor Card (short-haul: no RODS/ELD, no 30-minute break) — https://csa.fmcsa.dot.gov/Documents/HOS_VisorCard.pdf

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — US FAA, 14 CFR §61.113(i) (current as of the November 12, 2024 expansion)

=== 1. THE THREE ANSWERS ===

1) Maximum takeoff weight: not more than 12,500 lb — the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight (MTOW) must be 12,500 lb or less. 12,500 lb is the ceiling, not an allowance to operate at 12,500 lb.

2) Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: not more than 7 occupants. This is the aircraft's authorization (certificated/approved seating) limit, not a count of who is actually on board.

3) Passengers on board: no more than 6 passengers. This is the operating limit — who is actually on board, excluding the pilot and any other required flightcrew member.

The three numbers are mutually consistent by design: 6 passengers + 1 pilot = 7 occupants, which meets (does not exceed) the 7-occupant authorization ceiling.

=== 2. GOVERNING TEXT ===

14 CFR §61.113(i)(1) (current eCFR text):
"(i) A private pilot may act as pilot in command or serve as a required flightcrew member of an aircraft without holding a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter provided the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets the requirements of §61.23(c)(3), and complies with this section and all of the following conditions and limitations:
(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and"

FAA BasicMed program page, "Aircraft Requirements":
- "Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants"
- "Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds"

FAA Notice N 8000.386, citing PL 118-63 §828 (FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, "Expansion of BasicMed"), applicable on or after November 12, 2024:
- "The aircraft is authorized to carry no more than seven occupants,"
- "The aircraft has an MTOW of no more than 12,500 pounds, and"
- "The aircraft is operated with no more than six passengers on board."

=== 3. HOW EACH TERM IS TO BE APPLIED ===

(a) "Maximum takeoff weight" = maximum CERTIFICATED takeoff weight. It is a property of the aircraft (from its Type Certificate Data Sheet / AFM limitations), not the weight on the day of the flight. A 12,500 lb airplane flown light — say, at 9,000 lb actual takeoff weight — is still ineligible. Conversely, an aircraft certificated at 12,500 lb or below is eligible on the weight test regardless of how heavy it is loaded on a given flight (subject to its own W&B limits). The test is "not more than," so an aircraft certificated at exactly 12,500 lb passes.

(b) "Authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants" = the aircraft's certification/authorization limit on the number of persons it may carry. 'Occupants' includes the pilot and any other required flightcrew member. Sources for this figure:
- Type-certificated aircraft: the maximum seating capacity stated in the FAA Type Certificate Data Sheet (TCDS) and/or the AFM/Limitations section.
- Experimental/amateur-built and other special-airworthiness aircraft: the occupant limitation stated in the aircraft's Operating Limitations (typically a "not more than N persons" line).
- The test is the aircraft's authorization, not the load on the flight. An 8-seat airplane cannot be flown under BasicMed even with only 6 people on board, because it is "authorized to carry" 8.
- Exactly 7 authorized occupants passes ("not more than 7").

(c) "No more than 6 passengers on board" = the actual operating load, counting passengers only. Passengers = occupants other than the pilot and other required flightcrew. Exactly 6 passengers passes.

Practical interaction of (b) and (c):
- 1 pilot + 6 passengers = 7 occupants → compliant (both limits met exactly).
- 2 pilots (e.g., a second pilot acting as a required flightcrew member, or a safety pilot) + 6 passengers = 8 occupants → NON-compliant: the 6-passenger cap is met but the 7-occupant authorization is exceeded. With two pilots, the maximum passenger load is 5.
- 1 pilot + 5 passengers in a 6-occupant airplane → compliant on both.

=== 4. COMMON MISREADINGS TO AVOID ===

- BasicMed does not authorize an aircraft above 12,500 lb MTOW no matter how it is loaded.
- The 7-occupant number is not a passenger allowance. Passengers cap at 6.
- A high-seat-count aircraft does not become eligible by flying with few people aboard; the "authorized to carry" test is certification-based.
- BasicMed is an alternative to holding a medical certificate; it does not restrict the aircraft a medically certificated pilot may fly. The same pilot may fly a larger aircraft whenever a valid medical certificate is held.
- The limits are per-pilot and per-flight: each flight must independently satisfy the weight, occupant, passenger and other §61.113(i) conditions.
- The weight/occupant figures are US federal. A flight outside the United States is outside the scope of §61.113(i) (see the 'within the United States' operating condition below), and foreign authorities may not accept BasicMed.

=== 5. DATE / VERSION CONTROL (critical — the numbers changed) ===

- On or after November 12, 2024 (PL 118-63 §828): 12,500 lb MTOW / 7 occupants authorized / 6 passengers. THIS IS THE CURRENT ANSWER.
- Before November 12, 2024 (original FESSA 2016 BasicMed): 6,000 lb MTOW / 6 occupants authorized / 5 passengers. SUPERSEDED — historical only.
Any flight conducted before November 12, 2024 is judged against the older figures; any flight on or after that date is judged against 12,500 / 7 / 6. Confirm the effective date before applying the numbers to a specific flight that straddles the change.

=== 6. ADJACENT §61.113(i) AIRCRAFT/OPERATING CONDITIONS (context, not part of the three asks) ===

§61.113(i)(1) also excludes transport category rotorcraft certified under part 29.
§61.113(i)(2) requires the aircraft to be operated within the United States, at an indicated airspeed of not more than 250 knots, and at an altitude of not more than 18,000 ft MSL.
§61.113(i) also bars acting as PIC or a required flightcrew member for compensation or hire, and bars carrying passengers or property for compensation or hire.
Pilot-side prerequisites (not aircraft limits): valid US driver's license; §61.23(c)(3) eligibility including having held an FAA medical certificate after July 15, 2006; completion of the BasicMed medical education course; a physical examination by a state-licensed physician within the preceding 48 months; and the associated self-certification/consent items.

=== 7. PROCEDURE TO VERIFY A SPECIFIC AIRCRAFT ===

1. Obtain the aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight from the TCDS (or, for special-airworthiness aircraft, the Operating Limitations / AFM). Confirm it is <= 12,500 lb.
2. Obtain the authorized occupant count from the TCDS maximum seating capacity, the AFM Limitations section, or (E-AB/LSA/special) the Operating Limitations. Confirm it is <= 7.
3. Confirm the aircraft is not a part 29 transport category rotorcraft.
4. Plan the load so that the number of persons on board other than the pilot/required flightcrew is <= 6, and total persons on board is <= the lesser of 7 and the aircraft's authorized occupant count.
5. Confirm the intended flight is within the US, at or below 18,000 ft MSL and 250 KIAS, and is not for compensation or hire.
6. Record the basis (TCDS/AFM revision date) in the flight-planning record so the determination is reproducible.

Illustrative outcomes (verify each against the actual TCDS before relying on it):
- Cessna 172/182 class (4 occupants, MTOW ~2,550-3,100 lb): eligible.
- Cessna 340 class (6 occupants, MTOW just under 6,000 lb): eligible; was also eligible pre-Nov-2024.
- TBM 700/850 class single-engine turboprop (6 occupants, MTOW in the ~6,600-7,400 lb range): eligible now; was NOT eligible under the pre-Nov-2024 6,000 lb limit.
- Piper PA-31 Navajo class (typically 8 occupants, MTOW ~6,500 lb): NOT eligible — passes the 12,500 lb weight test but fails the 7-occupant authorization test.

=== 8. BOTTOM LINE ===

Under current US BasicMed (14 CFR §61.113(i), post-November 12, 2024): the aircraft must have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 lb, must be authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, and must be operated with no more than 6 passengers on board.

question: M3
answer:
FEDERAL HOURS-OF-SERVICE LIMITS — PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV (MOTORCOACH), 49 CFR 395.5(a)

== ANSWER TABLE ==

Ask 1 — How many hours may the driver drive?
  VALUE: 10 hours (maximum driving time).
  Basis: 49 CFR 395.5(a) — a driver of a passenger-carrying CMV may not drive more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

Ask 2 — After how many consecutive hours off duty?
  VALUE: 8 consecutive hours off duty (minimum qualifying rest).
  Basis: 49 CFR 395.5(a) — the 8 consecutive hours off duty is the rest period that must precede the driving and on-duty allowances; the clocks restart when the driver next comes on duty.

Ask 3 — After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive?
  VALUE: 15 hours on duty.
  Basis: 49 CFR 395.5(a) — no driving after the driver has been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

All three figures come from the same subsection and are interdependent: 8 consecutive hours off duty resets the clock; from the moment the driver next comes on duty, they get a 15-hour on-duty window, inside which no more than 10 hours may be driving.

== 1. HOW THE THREE NUMBERS WORK TOGETHER ==

The regulation is written as a single sentence with two prohibitions, and it is a mistake to read the three numbers as independent allowances.

(a) The 8-hour break is a gate, not a target. It must be at least 8 consecutive hours, and the driver must be relieved of all duty for the whole period. Eight hours of 'not driving' — e.g., riding in the passenger seat, doing paperwork, or waiting on call — does not qualify. The period must be off duty (sleeper-berth time may be combined with off-duty time only under the sleeper-berth provision in § 395.1(g)(3); see section 4).

(b) The 15-hour figure is elapsed clock time, not 15 hours of work. The window opens when the driver comes on duty after the 8-hour break and runs continuously regardless of what the driver is doing. Every on-duty minute that is not driving — pre-trip inspection, fueling, loading and unloading passengers, ticketing, paperwork, mechanical trouble, waiting at a terminal while still on duty — consumes window without consuming the 10 driving hours. A driver who spends 6 hours on duty not driving has only 9 hours of window left and can therefore drive at most 9 hours that day, not 10.

(c) The 10-hour figure is a cap on driving time inside the window. It is reachable only if no more than 5 hours of the 15-hour window is spent on duty not driving. Whichever limit is hit first governs.

(d) 'On duty' means all time from coming on duty until being relieved of duty, including driving, and includes the time the driver is required to be in readiness to work. It does not include bona fide off-duty time or qualifying sleeper-berth time.

== 2. WORKED EXAMPLE ==

Driver goes off duty at 20:00 Monday and is off duty until 06:00 Tuesday — 10 consecutive hours, which satisfies the 8-hour requirement with margin.
  - 06:00 Tuesday: on duty. The 15-hour window is now running and will close at 21:00.
  - 06:00–06:30: pre-trip inspection (on duty, not driving).
  - 06:30–12:30: driving, 6 hours. Cumulative driving 6; window used 6.5.
  - 12:30–13:30: lunch, off duty — this does not pause the 15-hour window; it only stops the driving clock.
  - 13:30–17:30: driving, 4 hours. Cumulative driving 10 — the 10-hour driving cap is now exhausted. No further driving this duty period.
  - 17:30–19:00: on duty not driving (post-trip, paperwork).
  - 21:00: the 15-hour window closes. Even if only 8 hours of driving had been used, no driving after 21:00.
  - Next driving requires a new qualifying rest: at least 8 consecutive hours off duty (or the sleeper-berth equivalent under section 4).

== 3. LIMITS THAT CAN STOP DRIVING EARLIER ==

These do not change the three answers, but they bind before 10 or 15 hours is reached:

- Weekly/biweekly ceiling, § 395.5(b): no driving after 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days, or 70 hours on duty in 8 consecutive days, whichever the carrier operates under. A driver can be fully compliant with the 10/8/15 daily limits and still be prohibited from driving by this cap. (Flag: the precise 60/70 text and whether a 34-hour restart is available to passenger carriers was not verified in the source set — verify against § 395.5(b) before relying on it.)
- Adverse driving conditions, § 395.1(b): permits not more than 2 additional hours beyond the maximum time allowed under § 395.5(a) to complete the run or reach a place of safety. Practical outer ceiling: 12 driving hours and driving no later than the end of the 17th hour. It applies only where the conditions were not known and not reasonably knowable before the duty day began (or before driving after a qualifying rest break or sleeper-berth period). It is an emergency completion allowance, not an extension a carrier can plan into a schedule. (Flag: whether the exception extends the on-duty window as well as the driving limit should be re-verified against the § 395.1(b) text.)
- Out-of-service orders, § 395.13: a driver declared out of service for HOS violations may not drive until the condition is corrected.
- Company policy and state law may be stricter (see section 6).

== 4. SLEEPER-BERTH PROVISION FOR PASSENGER CMVs, § 395.1(g)(3) ==

For a passenger-carrying CMV equipped with a sleeper berth, the equivalent of 8 consecutive hours off duty may be accumulated either by at least 8 consecutive hours off duty plus sleeper-berth time, or by two rest periods in the sleeper berth, provided:
  (i) neither rest period is shorter than 2 hours;
  (ii) the driving time in the periods immediately before and after each rest period, added together, does not exceed 10 hours;
  (iii) the on-duty time in the periods immediately before and after each rest period, added together, includes no driving after the 15th hour; and
  (iv) the driver may not return to driving under the normal § 395.5 limits without first taking at least 8 consecutive hours off duty, at least 8 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth, or a combination of the two.
This provision changes how the 8-hour rest may be assembled; it does not raise the 10-hour or 15-hour figures. A driver splitting rest this way must still satisfy (ii) and (iii) on every cycle.

== 5. DO NOT CONFUSE WITH PROPERTY-CARRYING RULES ==

The property-carrier limits in § 395.3 are different, and quoting them to a motorcoach driver is the most common error in this area. They are shown here only as a contrast; they are NOT the answer to this request.

  Element                      | Passenger CMV (§ 395.5(a)) | Property CMV (§ 395.3) — NOT applicable here
  Maximum driving              | 10 hours                   | 11 hours
  On-duty window after rest   | 15 hours                   | 14 hours
  Minimum reset off duty      | 8 consecutive hours        | 10 consecutive hours
  Weekly ceiling               | 60/7 or 70/8               | 60/7 or 70/8

If the vehicle in question is in fact property-carrying, the three answers would be 11 driving hours, 10 consecutive hours off duty, and a 14-hour window. Confirm the vehicle class before applying either table.

== 6. JURISDICTION AND SCOPE CAVEATS ==

- These are the US federal rules and apply to interstate operation of a passenger-carrying CMV. If the operation never crosses a state line and is not otherwise in interstate commerce, a state intrastate HOS rule may apply and may differ from 10/8/15. No state-specific intrastate rule was verified in this work; the three values above should not be applied to a purely intrastate operation without checking the state rule.
- The short-haul exception in § 395.1(e) is framed for property-carrying CMVs. Do not assume a motorcoach qualifies; verify before relying on it.
- The request asks only for the three daily limits. It does not cover drug and alcohol testing, CDL qualifications, passenger endorsement, or vehicle inspection requirements.

== 7. RECORDKEEPING ==

Drivers subject to part 395 must record duty status and must generally use an electronic logging device under subpart B of part 395, retaining records of duty status for six months. Paper records are permitted only where a specific exception applies. The ELD must be used to demonstrate the 10-hour, 8-hour, and 15-hour compliance described above; the device flags the 15-hour window and the 10-hour driving cap.

== 8. GROUNDING AND VERIFICATION STATUS ==

- The 10-hour, 8-hour, and 15-hour values are stated in the researched source answer with a citation to 49 CFR 395.5, and are consistent with each other as checked above.
- The sleeper-berth mechanics in section 4 are directly supported by the quoted regulatory passage from the eCFR part 395 page (§ 395.1(g)(3)).
- Items flagged unverified: the verbatim text of § 395.5(a) was not returned as a direct quote (the retrieved quote covers § 395.1(g)(3)); the 60/70-hour provision and any restart availability for passenger carriers; and the precise scope of the adverse-driving-conditions extension as it applies to the 15-hour window. Before using this answer for an enforcement, audit, or citation-response purpose, re-verify those three points against the current eCFR text of §§ 395.1 and 395.5.

== 9. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A DRIVER ==

A motorcoach driver may drive 10 hours, must have at least 8 consecutive hours off duty before starting the next duty period, and may not drive after the 15th hour on duty following that 8-hour break — subject also to the 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day ceiling.
cautions: The answer gives 15 hours for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: M5
answer:
GOVERNING RULE: 14 CFR § 135.273, 'Duty period limitations and rest requirements: flight attendants' (Part 135, Subpart F). Applies to a flight attendant as defined in § 135.273(a) — a crewmember other than a flight crewmember, designated by the certificate holder to perform flight attendant duties and appropriately trained and qualified. FAA guidance confirms the reach of the rule: 'any individual on a part 135 operation who fits the flight-attendant definition of § 135.273(a) is subject to the flight, duty, and rest rules of § 135.273.'

ANSWER 1 — BASELINE REST: 9 consecutive hours.
Rule text, § 135.273(b)(2): 'Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. This rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

ANSWER 2 — PERMITTED REDUCTION: to 8 consecutive hours, and only conditionally.
Rule text, § 135.273(b)(3): 'The rest period required under paragraph (b)(2) of this section may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; this subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.'

So the reduction is a fixed floor (8 hours), not a percentage and not a discretionary sliding scale. It is available in only two modes — 'scheduled' (planned that way in the pairing) or 'reduced' (applied to an already-built schedule) — and in either mode the four conditions below are mandatory.

FOUR CONDITIONS ON THE 8-HOUR REDUCTION (all must hold, conjunctively):
1. The reduced rest itself must be at least 8 consecutive hours.
2. A subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours must be given.
3. That 10-hour rest must be scheduled to BEGIN no later than 24 hours after the BEGINNING of the reduced rest period (clock runs from the start of the 8-hour rest, not from its end, and not from the end of duty).
4. That 10-hour rest must occur between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period — i.e., it cannot be merged into, or counted as, the reduced rest, and it must sit before the next duty period begins.

WORKED SCHEDULING ARITHMETIC (verify pattern, not a mandate):
- Duty period ends 20:30 on Day 1. Reduced rest begins 21:00 Day 1, runs 8 h to 05:00 Day 2. Compliant on condition 1.
- Condition 3 clock: 21:00 Day 1 + 24 h = 21:00 Day 2 deadline for the 10-hour subsequent rest to BEGIN.
- Therefore the Day 2 duty period must be complete and the 10-hour rest must start by 21:00 Day 2. If it starts at 21:00 Day 2, it runs to 07:00 Day 3. Compliant on conditions 2, 3 and 4.
- Consequence the scheduler must respect: the reduction is not free. It compresses the following day's duty window, because the 10-hour compensatory rest must be on the clock within 24 hours of the reduced rest's start. A pairing that uses 8-hour reduced rest and then runs a long Day 2 duty will violate condition 3 even though the 8 hours themselves were given.

WHAT 'REST' MUST BE: a scheduled period, at least the stated number of CONSECUTIVE hours, free of all duty, positioned between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. It is a protected scheduled interval, not merely leftover time; the operator's manual should define rest consistently with this (continuous, uninterrupted, free from all duty, including administrative and positioning/ deadhead assignments unless the manual provides otherwise).

SCOPE LIMITS ON THIS ANSWER (state them to the crew scheduler):
- The 9/8-hour figures apply to a SCHEDULED duty period of 14 hours or less, as the question posits. They are not a rule for a duty period exceeding 14 hours; if the actual or scheduled duty exceeds 14 hours, do not apply this answer — return to § 135.273(b)(1) and the operator's manual, because a different provision governs and this summary does not establish it.
- 9 hours is a regulatory MINIMUM, not a target. The certificate holder's manual, OpSpecs, or a collective bargaining agreement may impose a longer, non-reducible rest period; where they do, the stricter term controls and the 8-hour reduction may be unavailable. Confirm the operator's manual and any CBA before building to 8.
- The question is answered against the FAA Part 135 baseline only; no state, foreign, or contractual minimum is assessed here.
- Dual-qualified crew: if this person also serves as a flight crewmember, the flight crew rest rule in § 135.267 (10 consecutive hours of rest within 24 hours, with its own reduction mechanics) also applies, and the binding rest would exceed the 9 hours stated here. Verify the person's crew status before applying either number.
- If the person is not in fact a required/designated flight attendant under the operator's manual and aircraft, § 135.273 does not reach them and this answer does not apply.

RECORDKEEPING AND IMPLEMENTATION: record scheduled and actual duty periods and rest periods for each flight attendant per the certificate holder's recordkeeping obligations under Part 135 and its manual; retain the pairing/build records that show (a) the reduced rest was at least 8 consecutive hours, (b) the 10-hour subsequent rest was given, (c) its start time relative to the start of the reduced rest, and (d) that it fell before the next duty period. Flag in the scheduling system any pairing using 8-hour reduced rest so the 24-hour compensatory clock can be checked automatically at build time, and again at post-flight audit against actual times.

COMMON ERRORS TO REJECT:
- Treating 8 hours as the normal rest after a 14-hour-or-less duty (it is 9; 8 requires the compensatory package).
- Measuring the 24-hour clock from the END of the reduced rest or from the end of duty.
- Counting the 10-hour compensatory rest as satisfying the next duty period's own 9-hour rest when the two overlap improperly, or placing the 10-hour rest after the subsequent duty period begins.
- Reducing to 8 where the manual or CBA sets a non-reducible higher minimum.
- Applying these flight-attendant figures to flight crew, whose rest minimum is 10 hours under § 135.267.

question: M7
answer:
ANSWER

1. Current specification of HTTP/2: RFC 9113, "HTTP/2" (HTTP WG / httpbis, June 2022, Internet Standards Track). It is the core HTTP/2 protocol specification and the successor to RFC 7540.

2. RFC 9113 obsoletes exactly two RFCs:
   - RFC 7540 — "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)" (May 2015)
   - RFC 8740 — "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2" (February 2020)

Verbatim from the RFC Editor record (https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/): "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

That sentence answers both asks; the second ask is therefore not dependent on a separate, weaker source.


SCOPE DECISIONS (explicit, so the answer can be checked against its own premises)

- "Current" = the document the RFC Editor currently lists as the active, non-obsoleted HTTP/2 core specification, checked against the live RFC Editor / IETF Datatracker record at answer time. Not a snapshot from memory.
- "Obsoletes" = the formal RFC Editor `Obsoletes:` header field / Datatracker `obsoletes` metadata, not informal succession and not "Updates".
- The obsoletes list is the DIRECT list stated by RFC 9113. There is no transitive tail to expand: RFC 7540 obsoleted nothing, and RFC 8740 obsoleted nothing, so "direct only" and "full chain" produce the identical set {7540, 8740}. The ambiguity in the plan's open questions is therefore moot for this particular answer.
- RFCs that merely UPDATE RFC 9113 (if any) are out of scope by the stated assumptions; they do not change the Obsoletes answer.


WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THE LIST (common-error guards)

- RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2) is NOT obsoleted by RFC 9113. HPACK is still the current header-compression spec and RFC 9113 normatively references it. Do not add 7541.
- RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics) and RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1) are sibling documents published in the same June 2022 httpbis batch. RFC 9113 does not obsolete them, and they do not obsolete it.
- RFC 7301 (ALPN), RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3), RFC 9000/9114 (QUIC / HTTP/3) are referenced, not obsoleted.
- RFC 8740 is in the list even though it is a small TLS-profile document, because RFC 9113 folds its content in (HTTP/2 over TLS 1.3 with the mandatory cipher-suite restriction removed) and formally obsoletes it.


PROVENANCE — RFC 9113 header fields to expect

  Request for Comments: 9113
  Category: Standards Track
  ISSN: 2070-1721
  Obsoletes: 7540, 8740
  Updates: (none)
  Title: HTTP/2
  Publication date: June 2022
  Stream: IETF (HTTP Working Group, httpbis)
  DOI: 10.17487/RFC9113

A record showing `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740` and no `Obsoleted-By:` is the confirmation that the answer is current.


VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (re-runnable; do this before publishing the answer, because "current" is time-sensitive)

Step 1 — Confirm 9113 is still current and get its obsoletes list from the authoritative machine-readable record:

  curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' \
    https://datatracker.ietf.org/api/v1/doc/document/rfc9113/ \
  | jq '{name, title, std_level, obsoletes, updates, expires: .expires}'

Expected: name="rfc9113", title="HTTP/2", std_level containing "ps" (Proposed Standard / Standards Track), obsoletes=[7540, 8740], updates=[] (or empty).

Step 2 — Confirm nothing has obsoleted 9113 since:

  curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' \
    'https://datatracker.ietf.org/api/v1/doc/relateddocument/?relationship=obs&target__name=rfc9113&format=json' \
  | jq '.objects | length'

Expected: 0. A non-zero count means RFC 9113 has itself been obsoleted and the whole answer must be recomputed from the new document's Obsoletes field.

Step 3 — Human-readable cross-check of the same fact on the RFC Editor side:

  curl -s https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9113/ | grep -i -E 'obsolet|updates'

Expected to surface: "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

Step 4 — Confirm the two obsoleted documents are indeed dead ends (so the set is closed under succession):

  for r in 7540 8740; do
    curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' \
      https://datatracker.ietf.org/api/v1/doc/document/rfc$r/ \
    | jq '{name, obsoletes, obsoleted_by: [.related[:] | .[]? | select(.relationship=="obs") | .target.name]}'
  done

Expected: RFC 7540 obsoletes nothing; RFC 8740 obsoletes nothing. Their successors are RFC 9113 only.

Step 5 — Negative check on the common mistake (HPACK must NOT appear):

  curl -s -H 'Accept: application/json' \
    https://datatracker.ietf.org/api/v1/doc/document/rfc7541/ \
  | jq '[.related[]? | select(.relationship=="obs") | .target.name]'

Expected: does not include rfc9113. RFC 7541 remains current.


STALENESS / FAILURE MODES (how this answer becomes wrong, and the tripwire for each)

- A future RFC obsoletes RFC 9113 (e.g., a further httpbis revision). Tripwire: Step 2 returns > 0. Remedy: replace 9113 with the new number and re-read that document's Obsoletes field; the obsoleted set would then likely become {7540, 8740, 9113} or whatever the new header states — do not carry the old set forward by assumption.
- Conflating "Updates" with "Obsoletes". Tripwire: any document listing `Updates: 9113` (for example work on the HTTP priority scheme) is NOT added to the answer. The answer only changes if the `Obsoletes:` field changes.
- Confusing the HTTP/2 core spec with the wider HTTP suite. Tripwire: RFC 9110/9112 appear in the same publication batch; if a draft answer names them as obsoleted by 9113, it is wrong.


ONE-LINE RESTATEMENT FOR CITATION

HTTP/2 is currently specified by RFC 9113 (June 2022), which obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.

question: M9
answer:
# UK National Minimum Wage rates from 1 April 2026 — Policy note

## 1. The answer

| Band | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage — **21 and over** | **£12.71** | £12.21 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) |
| National Minimum Wage — **18 to 20** | **£10.85** | £10.00 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) |

Both figures are the **statutory** rates as legislated, not Low Pay Commission recommendations awaiting adoption. They are gross headline hourly rates in pounds sterling, UK-wide (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland), with no adjustment for accommodation offset or deductions.

## 2. Legal and evidential basis

- **Instrument:** The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026. Regulation 2(2) increases the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 or over from £12.21 to £12.71 per hour. Regulation 2(3)(a) increases the rate for workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21 from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour.
- **Official rates table (GOV.UK, National Minimum Wage rates):** April 2026 row reads 21 and over £12.71 / 18 to 20 £10.85 / Under 18 £8 / Apprentice £8.
- **GOV.UK policy publication, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026':** "From 1 April 2026, all rates of the National Minimum Wage, including the National Living Wage, increase."
- The two sources agree to the penny, so there is no discrepancy to resolve.

## 3. Effective date and the operative payroll rule

The rates take effect **1 April 2026**. The operative rule for payrollers is not the calendar date but the pay period: **the new rates must be used from the first pay period starting on or after 1 April 2026** (GOV.UK, April 2026 issue of the Employer Bulletin). A four-weekly or monthly payroll whose period straddles 1 April therefore applies the old rates to that period and the new rates from the next period's start.

## 4. Age-band definitions applying from April 2026

The GOV.UK rates table shows four bands for April 2026: 21 and over; 18 to 20; Under 18; Apprentice. The legislation confirms the adult rate applies to workers aged 21 or over and the 18–20 rate to workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21. No restructuring of the band boundaries is in force for April 2026.

Operational point: the band that applies is determined by the worker's age, and where a worker crosses a band boundary part-way through a pay reference period the higher rate generally takes effect from the start of the next pay reference period. Confirm the exact wording against the 2015 Regulations as amended by the 2026 instrument before relying on that rule in an individual case — it is stated here as the expected position, not as a quoted provision.

## 5. Adjacent figures (not requested — flagged for completeness only)

- Under 18 rate from April 2026: £8.00.
- Apprentice rate from April 2026: £8.00.
- The **accommodation offset** is set separately from the wage bands and is not quoted here because the 2026 figure was not in the sourced material. If the requester needs it, take it from the same amending instrument rather than inferring it.
- The **London Living Wage** is a separate voluntary scheme run by the Living Wage Foundation and is not part of this answer.

## 6. Worked checks (for a 37.5-hour week)

- 21 and over: 12.71 × 37.5 = **£476.63** per week (rounded to the nearest penny). Annualised on the same basis, 12.71 × 1,950 hours = **£24,784.50**.
- 18 to 20: 10.85 × 37.5 = **£406.88** per week. Annualised, 10.85 × 1,950 hours = **£21,157.50**.
- Note on rounding: the annual figures are computed from the hourly rate × 1,950 hours, not from the rounded weekly figure × 52 (which would give £24,784.76 and £21,157.76 respectively). Use one basis consistently in any pay modelling.

## 7. Implementation checklist for an employer

1. Update payroll rate tables to £12.71 (21+) and £10.85 (18–20) with an effective-from date keyed to the first pay period starting on or after 1 April 2026, not to 1 April itself.
2. Re-test every worker sitting within 5% of the old floor — the 18–20 band rose 8.5%, so differentials and junior-to-adult progressions may now be compressed or inverted.
3. Check age-band assignment for anyone turning 18 or 21 in the first quarter of the 2026/27 year.
4. Re-check that deductions and required payments (uniform, tools, accommodation) do not push any worker below the new floor; the accommodation offset is treated separately from the hourly rate.
5. Confirm apprentice eligibility (apprentice rate applies only within the defined apprenticeship conditions and age/first-year limits) rather than assuming it.
6. Record the source and date of the rates used, so the decision is auditable when the next amendment is made.

## 8. Scope of this note

This note supplies the two requested statutory rates and the minimum operational context needed to apply them. It does not compute net pay, does not address National Insurance or pension thresholds, and does not quote the 2026 accommodation offset or London Living Wage figures, which were not available in the sourced material.

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (RODS/ELD-EXEMPT) — RADIUS AND RELEASE WINDOW

1. ANSWERS

Ask 1 — Radius: 150 air miles. The driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation states the equivalent in statute miles in parentheses: 172.6 statute miles (1 air mile = 1.15078 statute miles; 150 x 1.15078 = 172.617, rounded to 172.6 in the text). The 150 air-mile figure is the operative measurement; 172.6 statute miles is the same distance expressed differently, not a second threshold.

Ask 2 — Release from work: 14 consecutive hours. The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The 14 hours runs from the start of the workday (reporting for duty) to release at the normal work reporting location — it is a wall-clock window for the whole duty period, not 14 hours of driving.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT — 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), '150 air-mile radius driver'

'(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours; ...'

Source of the quoted language: eCFR, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) (http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/section-395.1), fetched 2026-11-16T01:35:14Z, sha256 1f7674313f0d. Corroborating sources: GovInfo CFR-2025-title49-vol5 sec. 395-1 PDF; FMCSA 'Drivers Guide to Hours of Service' (2022-04-28); FMCSA HOS summary page; FMCSA HOS Visor Card. Note that the first research pass was marked unverified (no quoted passage); the second pass produced the verbatim quote above, so the answer rests on quoted regulatory text, not on a paraphrase.

3. CARVE-OUT THAT LIMITS ASK 2

The 14-consecutive-hour release requirement in (e)(1)(ii) is stated 'except a driver-salesperson.' A driver-salesperson therefore is not bound by the 14-hour release condition, though still bound by the 150 air-mile radius condition in (i) and the off-duty separation condition in (iii). For every driver other than a driver-salesperson, 14 consecutive hours is the correct bound.

4. OTHER QUALIFYING CONDITIONS IN THE SAME PARAGRAPH (not answers to asks 1 or 2 — listed so the exception is not half-applied)

- Exemption scope: the exception exempts only from 49 CFR 395.8 (records of duty status) and 395.11 (supporting documents). It is not a general hours-of-service exemption.
- Off-duty separation: at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14 hours on duty for property-carrying drivers; at least 8 consecutive hours off duty for passenger-carrying drivers (395.1(e)(1)(iii)). These 10/8 figures are the rest-period requirement and are distinct from, and must not be confused with, the 14-consecutive-hour release window that answers ask 2.
- Still-applicable limits: because the exemption reaches only 395.8 and 395.11, the driver remains subject to the 11-hour driving limit (395.3(a)(1)), the 30-minute break (395.3(a)(3)(ii)), and the 60/70-hour limits (395.3(b)). The general 14-hour driving window of 395.3(a)(2) is in practice subsumed by the stricter 'released from work within 14 consecutive hours' condition.
- Non-CDL drivers: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(2) is a separate short-haul provision for drivers of property-carrying CMVs not requiring a CDL, with its own additional conditions. The two values asked here are governed by (e)(1); anyone applying the exception to a non-CDL driver must read (e)(2) in the current text before relying on it.

5. VERSION / CURRENCY (the main failure mode for this question)

Answer reflects the current 49 CFR 395.1 as amended by the FMCSA hours-of-service final rule effective September 29, 2020, which enlarged the short-haul exception from 100 air miles to 150 air miles and from 12 consecutive hours to 14 consecutive hours. Any source, training deck, or state handout stating 100 air miles and/or 12 consecutive hours is pre-2020 and superseded; do not use it. Verify currency by re-pulling eCFR 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) at time of use and checking the 'source'/'authority' citation line at the end of the section.

6. COMPLIANCE NOTE ON APPLICATION

Because the driver is exempt from keeping records of duty status, the carrier's evidence that the exception applies is necessarily indirect. To support the 150 air-mile and 14-hour determinations, retain the driver's designated normal work reporting location, dispatch/route data sufficient to show the operation stayed inside 150 air miles of that location, and clock or dispatch records showing start of duty and release at the reporting location each day. Measure the radius from the normal work reporting location, not from the driver's residence or the first stop; measure air miles (great-circle nautical miles), not road miles. If a day's operation falls outside the radius or past the 14th hour, the exception does not apply to that day and a record of duty status is required for it.

question: M1
answer:
# BasicMed aircraft operating limits (US FAA)

## 1. Answer — current limits

BasicMed does not change the aircraft's type certificate. It defines a class of aircraft (a "covered aircraft") that a pilot may operate while exercising private pilot privileges on the basis of a driver's license and self-certification instead of an FAA medical certificate. The aircraft limits are **per-flight operating limits**, set out in 14 CFR 61.113(i) and administered under 14 CFR Part 68.

| # | Limit | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum certificated takeoff weight of the aircraft | **12,500 lb** |
| 2 | Maximum number of occupants the aircraft may be **authorized under Federal law** to carry | **7 occupants** (including any required flightcrew members) |
| 3 | Maximum number of **passengers on board** | **6 passengers** |

Arithmetic check: the occupant ceiling is 7 **including** required flightcrew. With one pilot, 7 − 1 = 6 passengers, which matches the passenger limit exactly. The two numbers are different expressions of the same ceiling, not two independent limits.

## 2. Which figures apply — current vs. legacy

There are two figure sets in circulation, and both still appear in FAA-published material. They are not interchangeable:

| Limit | Current (FAA BasicMed page; FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024) | Legacy (AC 68-1A, 2017; original Part 68 / 61.113(i) rule text) |
|---|---|---|
| Max certificated takeoff weight | 12,500 lb | 6,000 lb |
| Max occupants aircraft may be authorized to carry | 7 (incl. required flightcrew) | 6 (incl. required flightcrew) |
| Max passengers on board | 6 | 5 |

Selection rule for the pilot in command:
- **Apply the current set (12,500 lb / 7 / 6)** where the FAA's current BasicMed guidance and the 2024 reauthorization amendments govern the flight. This is the answer to the question as asked today.
- **Apply the legacy set (6,000 lb / 6 / 5)** only if you are deliberately operating to the pre-2024 rule text as it still reads in AC 68-1A and, pending conforming amendment, in the codified regulation — i.e., the conservative posture. Operating to the lower set is always compliant with the higher set; the reverse is not.

Compliance note to record in any operation or training document: the FAA advisory circular AC 68-1 / AC 68-1A (2017) has not been revised to the new figures, so an inspector, insurer, or reviewer may quote 6,000 lb / 6 / 5 at you. Cite the source and date you relied on, and verify the current text of 14 CFR 61.113(i) on eCFR plus the FAA BasicMed page before the flight.

## 3. How each limit is measured (the part that is usually got wrong)

**Maximum certificated takeoff weight (12,500 lb).** This is the weight in the aircraft's type certificate / AFM / placards — the maximum certificated takeoff weight, not the actual ramp or takeoff weight on the day. An aircraft certificated at 12,500 lb or less qualifies even if it is light that day; an aircraft certificated above the limit does not qualify even if it is flown light.

**Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry (7).** This looks at what the aircraft is *authorized under Federal law* to carry — the certificated maximum occupancy, not the number of seats currently installed. Removing seats does not bring an aircraft under BasicMed. A type certificated for 8 or more occupants is excluded even if only two seats remain bolted in. "Including any required flightcrew members" means the pilot (and any second-in-command required by the AFM, type certificate, or operating rules) counts against the 7.

**Passengers on board (6).** "Passenger" means an occupant other than the pilot in command / required flightcrew. Consequence worth spelling out: if the aircraft requires two pilots, the required SIC is an occupant but not a passenger, so the practical passenger count drops to 5. Non-required extra pilots occupying seats are treated as passengers for this purpose.

## 4. Other conditions that must be met on the same flight

The aircraft limits are necessary but not sufficient. For the flight to be conducted under BasicMed, all of the following must also be true:

1. The pilot holds a valid US driver's license.
2. The pilot has completed the FAA BasicMed medical education course within the preceding 48 calendar months.
3. The pilot holds a Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist (CMEC) signed by a state-licensed physician within the preceding 48 calendar months.
4. The pilot has held a valid FAA medical certificate at some point after July 15, 2006, and has not had a medical certificate revoked, suspended, or withdrawn.
5. Any known medical condition is managed per the BasicMed conditions and limitations; any special-issuance history is handled as Part 68 requires.
6. The flight is operated under 14 CFR Part 91, not for compensation or hire, and not in an operation requiring more than private pilot privileges.
7. The flight is within the United States. BasicMed is a US construct and is not ICAO-recognized; verify acceptance before any flight into Canada, Mexico, the Bahamas, or elsewhere.
8. The aircraft is a "covered aircraft" satisfying items 1–3 above.

A pilot who holds a current FAA medical certificate is not restricted by these aircraft limits and may fly larger aircraft under that certificate. The limits attach to the BasicMed pathway, not to the pilot permanently.

## 5. Verification steps before relying on this

1. Pull 14 CFR 61.113(i) on eCFR and read the definition of "covered aircraft" and the operating limits as currently codified.
2. Pull the FAA BasicMed page (faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med) and confirm the stated weight, occupant, and passenger figures.
3. Check AC 68-1A and the BasicMed FAQ for the legacy figures and note the date of the document, not just its number.
4. Confirm the specific aircraft's maximum certificated takeoff weight and certificated maximum occupancy from its AFM / type certificate data sheet / placards — not from a seat count or a listing site.
5. Record the source and access date in the flight or training record so the version question is answerable later.

question: M3
answer:
HOURS OF SERVICE FOR A DRIVER OF A PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV (MOTORCOACH) - US FEDERAL RULES

=====================================================================
1. SCOPE AND GOVERNING PROVISION
=====================================================================
Governing rule: 49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.' The section opens 'Subject to the exceptions and exemptions in 395.1,' so the numbers below are the base rule and are displaced or modified only where a 395.1 exception/exemption applies (see section 6).

Assumed scope (state these back to the client; the answer changes if they fail):
  (a) The driver operates a 'passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle' - per 49 CFR 390.5, a CMV designed to transport 16 or more passengers, including the driver (motorcoach, charter/tour bus, intercity bus).
  (b) Operation is in interstate commerce, so the federal rule governs directly.
  (c) No 395.1 exception or exemption applies (no emergency relief declaration under 390.23, no adverse driving conditions, no state-specific exception).
  (d) Current rule text as published on eCFR (no reliance on a superseded vintage).

If (b) fails - purely intrastate passenger operation - the state's own hours-of-service rule governs; many states incorporate 395.5 by reference (producing the same 10/8/15 numbers), but several do not, and the state rule controls. If (a) fails (fewer than 16 passengers), the vehicle may not be a CMV at all and federal HOS may not apply.

=====================================================================
2. THE THREE ANSWERS
=====================================================================

ASK 1 - Maximum driving time.
  10 hours. 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1): no motor carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV 'more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'
  This is DRIVING time only. It is not the length of the work day.

ASK 2 - Consecutive hours off duty required before driving.
  8 consecutive hours. The 8 hours must be consecutive and must be off duty; the 10-hour and 15-hour clocks both run from the end of that 8-hour period (395.5(a)(1)-(2)).

ASK 3 - Hours on duty after which driving is prohibited.
  15 hours. 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2): no driving 'for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'
  This is the on-duty window: it measures elapsed on-duty time from the start of the duty period, whether that time was spent driving or on duty not driving (loading, pre-trip, paperwork, dispatching, waiting on duty).

Interlock of the three: the 8 hours off duty starts the shift; within the shift the driver may accumulate at most 10 hours of driving and may not drive at all after the 15th hour of on-duty time, whichever binds first. Because 10 < 15, the driving cap normally binds first; the 15-hour window becomes binding when the driver has 5 or more hours of on-duty non-driving time before completing 10 driving hours.

=====================================================================
3. SEPARATE CUMULATIVE CAP (NOT the answer to ask 3, but it also prohibits driving)
=====================================================================
49 CFR 395.5(b): no driving, regardless of the number of motor carriers using the driver's services, after -
  (b)(1) having been on duty 60 hours in any 7 consecutive days, if the employing motor carrier does NOT operate CMVs every day of the week; or
  (b)(2) having been on duty 70 hours in any period of 8 consecutive days, if the employing motor carrier DOES operate CMVs every day of the week.
Notes for the engineer:
  - Which figure applies is a property of the CARRIER's operating schedule, not the driver's preference. Confirm the carrier's schedule in writing before dispatch planning.
  - These are ON-DUTY hours (driving plus other on-duty), counted over a rolling 7- or 8-day window, not a fixed calendar week.
  - 395.5 contains no 34-hour restart provision; the restart at 395.3(c) is written for property-carrying drivers. Do not assume a restart is available to a passenger-carrier driver - plan the rolling window.
  - 395.5 contains no 30-minute break requirement; the break at 395.3(a)(3)(ii) is property-carrying only.
  - 395.5 contains no sleeper-berth split; 395.1(g) is limited to property-carrying CMVs. A passenger-carrier driver therefore needs 8 CONSECUTIVE hours off duty - the 8 hours cannot be split into two qualifying berth periods the way a property driver can.

=====================================================================
4. DO NOT SUBSTITUTE THE PROPERTY-CARRYING NUMBERS
=====================================================================
The following are 49 CFR 395.3 (property-carrying) figures and are NOT applicable here: 11 hours driving; 14-hour on-duty window; 10 consecutive hours off duty; 30-minute break after 8 cumulative driving hours; 34-hour restart; sleeper-berth split rest. Any document, dispatch sheet, or ELD configuration that shows 11/14/10 for a motorcoach driver is misconfigured for the passenger rule.

=====================================================================
5. WORKED TIMELINE (verification of internal consistency)
=====================================================================
Driver goes off duty 22:00 and is off duty continuously until 06:00 (8 consecutive hours -> ask 2 satisfied).
  06:00  on duty. The 15-hour window (ask 3) runs to 21:00.
  06:00-06:30  pre-trip inspection, paperwork (on duty, not driving).
  06:30-12:00  driving = 5.5 h.
  12:00-12:45  lunch, off duty (does not count as driving, and does NOT extend the 15-hour window).
  12:45-17:15  driving = 4.5 h. Cumulative driving = 10.0 h -> ask 1 exhausted; no further driving even though only 11.25 h of the window has elapsed.
  Driving is prohibited at 17:15 by the 10-hour cap, and in any event at 21:00 by the 15-hour cap.
Check: 10.0 driving <= 15.0 window (consistent); 8.0 off duty immediately preceding (consistent). If instead the driver had 6 hours of on-duty non-driving time before finishing driving, the 15-hour cap would stop driving first - the two limits are independent and the earlier one controls.

=====================================================================
6. EXCEPTIONS THAT CAN MOVE THESE NUMBERS (check before relying on 10/8/15)
=====================================================================
49 CFR 395.5 is expressly subject to 395.1. Confirm each of the following before treating 10/8/15 as universal:
  - 395.1(b), adverse driving conditions: unforeseen conditions encountered during the run may permit driving for up to 2 additional hours beyond the 395.5(a) limits. It does not enlarge the 395.5(b) 60/70-hour caps. Verify the current text and the 'unforeseen' element before claiming it.
  - 390.23 emergency relief: only under a declared emergency and only for the relief granted; document the declaration.
  - State-specific and operation-specific exceptions within 395.1 (e.g., certain intrastate/Alaska/Hawaii provisions, school-bus operations) - check the current section text rather than assuming a general charter/tour exemption exists. There is no blanket charter or tour exemption from 395.5.
  - Driver qualifies for a records-of-duty-status exception (e.g., short-haul-type relief under 395.1(e)) - that changes the paperwork, not the 10/8/15 limits.

7. CITATIONS TO PUT IN THE DELIVERABLE
=====================================================================
  49 CFR 395.5(a)(1)  - 10 hours driving following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
  49 CFR 395.5(a)(2)  - no driving after 15 hours on duty following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

Off-duty breaks inside the shift do not extend the 15-hour window, and the 8 hours cannot be split.'

question: M5
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — 14 CFR § 135.273, flight attendant rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less (US on-demand charter operator, Part 135)

=== A. ANSWERS ===

1. Baseline rest: 9 consecutive hours. A flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours.

2. Reduction: to 8 consecutive hours, and only if the operator simultaneously provides a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours, scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period, and occurring between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period. If that compensatory condition is not met, there is no reduction and the 9-hour baseline governs. No reduction below 8 consecutive hours is authorized for this case by any provision of § 135.273.

=== B. REGULATORY BASIS (verbatim, primary source) ===

Authority: 14 CFR Part 135, Subpart F (Crewmember Flight Time and Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements), § 135.273 "Duty period limitations and rest time requirements."

§ 135.273(b)(2) — retrieved text, eCFR, sha256 88e87edd4ca6:
"(2) Except as provided in paragraph (b)(3) of this section, a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under paragraph (b)(1) of this section must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours."

§ 135.273(b)(3) — the cross-referenced exception that answers ask 2 (operative content; see Verification Register item V-1):
The rest period required by (b)(2) may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours; that subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Structural note for the file: the research summary supplied with this assignment stated that no reduced rest was verified for the 14-hours-or-less case. That conclusion is contradicted by the text it quotes. Paragraph (b)(2) is expressly written subject to an exception in (b)(3); a cross-referenced exception to a rest minimum is a reduced-rest provision. The correct reading is 9 hours reducible to 8, not 9 hours with no reduction. (b)(8) is a different provision, addressing the longer-duty-period case under (b)(7); it does not govern this fact pattern and its numbers are deliberately not restated here.

=== C. CONDITIONS FOR THE 8-HOUR REDUCTION (all four must be satisfied and documented) ===

C-1. The reduced rest is a single continuous block of at least 8 consecutive hours, free from all duty.
C-2. A subsequent (compensatory) rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours is provided.
C-3. That subsequent rest period is scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.
C-4. That subsequent rest period occurs between the completion of the scheduled duty period (the one that preceded the reduced rest) and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.
C-5. The reduction is applied period-by-period. It is not cumulative and cannot be banked, traded, or offset against another rest period.
C-6. Where the operator's FAA-accepted manual, operations specifications, LOA, or collective bargaining agreement is more restrictive than 9/8, the more restrictive figure governs. § 135.273 is a floor, not a ceiling.

=== D. WORKED COMPLIANCE EXAMPLE (arithmetic verified) ===

Scheduled duty D1 ends 20:00. Reduced rest begins 20:00 D1 and runs to 04:00 D2 = 8 consecutive hours (satisfies C-1).
Duty D2 runs 04:00 to 16:00 = 12 hours, which is within the '14 hours or less' band, so the same paragraph continues to govern.
Compensatory rest runs 16:00 D2 to 02:00 D3 = 10 consecutive hours (satisfies C-2).
Its start, 16:00 D2, is 20 hours after the reduced-rest start of 20:00 D1; 20 <= 24 (satisfies C-3).
It falls after completion of D1 and before the start of the next duty period at 02:00 D3 (satisfies C-4).
Result: compliant 8-hour reduction. Had the compensatory rest been scheduled to start at 21:00 D2 (25 hours after 20:00 D1), C-3 would fail and the pairing would be non-compliant even though 10 consecutive hours were eventually given.

=== E. SCOPE, EXCLUSIONS, INTERACTIONS ===

E-1. Applicability. § 135.273 governs flight attendants of Part 135 certificate holders. The rule is stated in terms of what the certificate holder must 'give' and 'schedule'; both the scheduling act and the actual provision must be satisfied.
E-2. Scheduled vs. actual duty period. The 14-hour band is set at scheduling. An actual overrun does not retroactively convert the pairing into the >14-hour regime, and the >14-hour regime does not retroactively cure a mis-scheduled pairing. Track scheduled and actual times separately.
E-3. What counts as rest. Rest is a continuous off-duty block. Time during which the flight attendant remains subject to the operator's control — required positioning/deadhead, on-call status, required ground training, or any assigned duty — is not rest. Whether required deadhead counts toward the 14-hour duty period itself is a separate question governed by the duty-period definition and the operator's manual/OpSpecs; confirm against the operator's GOM before relying on it (see V-3).
E-4. Dual-qualified personnel. A person who is also a flight crewmember must independently satisfy §§ 135.263–135.271 in addition to § 135.273. Compliance with one set does not excuse the other; the more restrictive applicable requirement controls.
E-5. Other parts. If any leg is conducted under Part 121, the Part 121 flight attendant rest rules apply to that flying and are outside this determination. Part 91 subpart K is likewise out of scope.
E-6. No FAA-approved deviation for this operator is assumed. An OpSpec, LOA, or manual provision can only tighten these minima, not relax them.

=== F. OPERATOR PROCEDURE (to be inserted into the GOM / crew scheduling SOP) ===

F-1. At pairing construction, tag every flight attendant duty period as '<=14 h' or '>14 h'. The <=14 h tag invokes the 9-hour default.
F-2. Default scheduling rule: insert a 9-consecutive-hour rest block between the end of the scheduled duty period and the start of the next duty period. No manual override without the F-3 record.
F-3. Reduced-rest record. Any use of the 8-hour reduction must be accompanied by a signed/electronic scheduling record capturing: reduced rest start and end; the 24-hour deadline (reduced rest start + 24:00); the compensatory rest start and end; the 10-hour minimum check; the 'between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period' check; and the identity of the scheduler. A pairing that fails any check must be rebuilt.
F-4. Trip check before release. The scheduler or dispatcher verifies that no rest block has been shortened to 8 hours without a matching, in-window 10-hour compensatory rest already built into the same or the next pairing.
F-5. Recordkeeping. Retain duty-period and rest records for each flight attendant as required by § 135.63 and the operator's FAA-accepted recordkeeping provisions, in a form producible to the FAA on request. Retention duration to be confirmed (V-4); do not adopt a number until confirmed.
F-6. Irregular operations. If an actual rest block is eroded below the scheduled figure, the crewmember is not released to the next duty period until the applicable minimum (9, or 8 with a compliant compensatory rest already given) is restored. Document the disruption.
F-7. Noncompliance exposure. A shorted rest period is an enforcement matter under § 135.273, not merely a policy lapse; it also creates a recordkeeping deficiency under § 135.63. Treat F-4 as a hard gate.

=== G. VERIFICATION REGISTER (one check each; none of these changes the answers unless the check fails) ===

V-1. Fetch the current text of § 135.273(b)(3) at https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/part-135/section-135.273 and confirm the four elements C-1 through C-4. Why: the (b)(3) text was not in the retrieved corpus, and the 8-hour figure rests on it. If (b)(3) is amended, the ask-2 value must be replaced with the amended figure; if (b)(3) were ever removed, ask 2 becomes 'no reduction available.' This is the single open evidentiary item.
V-2. Confirm the effective date / revision of Part 135 currently loaded in the operator's compliance program matches the eCFR point-in-time relied on here.
V-3. Confirm from the operator's GOM/OpSpecs how deadhead and on-call time are treated for duty-period computation.
V-4. Confirm the retention period for duty/rest records under § 135.63 and any applicable OpSpec.
V-5. Confirm no CBA or company policy imposes a rest minimum longer than 9/8; if it does, that figure supersedes for scheduling purposes.

=== H. CONFIDENCE ===

Ask 1 (9 consecutive hours): high — directly quoted primary text.
Ask 2 (8 consecutive hours with a 10-consecutive-hour compensatory rest beginning within 24 hours): high on substance, single-source-pending on text — established by the express (b)(3) cross-reference in the quoted (b)(2) and by the operative content of (b)(3); confirm via V-1 before publishing the GOM revision.
cautions: The answer gives 8 hours for ask 2, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: M7
answer:
# HTTP/2 current specification and its obsoletes

## Answers

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|-----|--------|
| 1 | Which RFC is the current specification of HTTP/2? | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2* (IETF, Standards Track / Proposed Standard, June 2022) |
| 2 | Which RFCs does it obsolete? | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** |

Short form: RFC 9113 is the current HTTP/2 specification; it obsoletes RFC 7540 (*HTTP/2*, the original 2015 specification) and RFC 8740 (*Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2*).

## 1. Current specification: RFC 9113

- **Document:** RFC 9113, title *HTTP/2*.
- **Stream:** IETF HTTP Working Group; published in the June 2022 HTTP set (RFC 9110 *HTTP Semantics*, RFC 9111 *HTTP Caching*, RFC 9112 *HTTP/1.1*, RFC 9113 *HTTP/2*, RFC 9114 *HTTP/3*).
- **Status:** Standards Track, Proposed Standard. This is the same maturity level RFC 7540 held, so the "latest published RFC" reading and the "highest standards-track level" reading of *current* converge on the same document — the ambiguity flagged in the request analysis does not change the answer here.
- **Why it is current and not RFC 7540:** RFC 7540 is explicitly marked as obsoleted by RFC 9113, and RFC 9113's own header and body state that it replaces RFC 7540. Any reference to RFC 7540 as *the* HTTP/2 specification is out of date.
- **Governing identifier for citation:** `RFC 9113`, DOI `10.17487/RFC9113`, canonical URI `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html`.

## 2. Obsoletes: RFC 7540 and RFC 8740

RFC 9113's front matter carries the header line:

```
Obsoletes: 7540, 8740
```

and the document body states verbatim:

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."

Breakdown of each entry:

| Obsoleted RFC | Title | What it was | Why RFC 9113 obsoletes it |
|---|---|---|---|
| **RFC 7540** | *Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)* | The original HTTP/2 specification (May 2015), which itself obsoleted RFC 1945-era work on the HTTP/2 line via SPDY-derived drafts | Superseded wholesale by the 2022 revision of the HTTP/2 protocol text |
| **RFC 8740** | *Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2* | A narrow 2020 update that removed the TLS 1.3 restriction on HTTP/2's TLS configuration (the "TLS 1.3 must not be used with HTTP/2" rule from RFC 7540 §9.2) | Its content was folded into RFC 9113's TLS section, so the standalone document is no longer needed |

**Direct chain only.** RFC 9113 is the terminal node of the HTTP/2 supersession chain for the purposes of this question: RFC 7540 → (obsoleted by) RFC 9113, and RFC 8740 → (obsoleted by) RFC 9113. No transitive expansion is made, because the ask is what the current specification obsoletes, not the full ancestry of HTTP/2 documents.

## 3. Scope decisions and explicit exclusions

These are the judgment calls the request left open; each is stated so the answer can be audited rather than guessed at.

1. **"Obsoletes" = the formal `Obsoletes:` header only**, not the `Updates:` relationships and not documents that are merely historically superseded. RFC 9113 carries no `Updates:` entries relevant to this count.
2. **RFC 7541 (HPACK) is NOT obsoleted by RFC 9113.** This is the most common error in this area: because RFC 7540 is obsoleted, people assume its companion header-compression spec went with it. It did not. RFC 9113 keeps HPACK as a separate, still-current specification and normatively references RFC 7541. RFC 7541 must therefore be excluded from the answer to ask 2.
3. **Errata do not change the identifier.** RFC 9113 has verified errata filed against it. Errata are corrections to a published RFC; they do not produce a new RFC number and do not alter the `Obsoletes:` list. If the asker needs the fully corrected text, the answer is "RFC 9113 plus its verified errata," still RFC 9113.
4. **Drafts are excluded.** No draft-ietf-httpbis-* document supersedes RFC 9113 as of this writing; drafts are not specifications in the RFC sense used here.
5. **Non-IETF documents are excluded.** The answer concerns IETF RFCs only.

## 4. Verification procedure (reproducible)

Anyone can confirm both values in under a minute:

1. Open `https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html` and read the header block. Confirm the title line `HTTP/2`, the `Obsoletes: 7540, 8740` line, and the Status-of-This-Memo section.
2. Or query the RFC Editor index / Datatracker: `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/` shows "Obsoletes: RFC 7540, RFC 8740" in the document metadata.
3. Cross-check the other direction: `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540/` shows "Obsoleted by: RFC 9113", and `https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8740/` likewise shows "Obsoleted by: RFC 9113". Reciprocal links in both directions are the strongest confirmation that the obsoletes relationship is real and complete.
4. To confirm nothing newer exists, search `https://www.rfc-editor.org/search/?q=HTTP%2F2` and check that no RFC published after 9113 claims to obsolete it. If a future RFC does so, the answer to ask 1 becomes that RFC and the answer to ask 2 becomes whatever its `Obsoletes:` header names.

## 5. Freshness note

The values above were confirmed against the RFC 9113 text and the RFC Editor/Datetracker metadata at the time of the source fetch (2026-11-16). RFC statuses are mutable: a future RFC could obsolete RFC 9113, and at that moment the correct answer to ask 1 changes and the answer to ask 2 becomes that successor's `Obsoletes:` list (which would include 9113). Step 4 above is the re-check to run if this answer is being reused much later. As of the check performed, no such successor exists, and RFC 9113 with obsoletes {7540, 8740} is the correct, current answer.
