UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES EFFECTIVE FROM 1 APRIL 2026 — HR/Payroll Note

1. DIRECT ANSWERS

| Band | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Change vs 2025 rate |
|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | £12.71 | +£0.50 (+4.1%) from £12.21 |
| National Minimum Wage — 18 to 20 year olds | £10.85 | +£0.85 (+8.5%) from £10.00 |

Both figures are gross pounds sterling per hour worked. They are the statutory minima set under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 and uprated by the annual amending regulations (the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026). They are not the voluntary Living Wage Foundation 'Real Living Wage' and must not be conflated with it.

2. FULL 2026 RATE TABLE (for completeness and to prevent band misassignment)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | 2025 rate | Increase |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £12.21 | +4.1% |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | +8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | +6.0% |
| Accommodation offset (daily limit on charges that may reduce NMW pay) | £11.10 | £10.66 | +4.1% |

Consistency checks passed: each 2026 rate minus its stated cash increase equals the published 2025 rate; each percentage equals the cash increase divided by the 2025 rate to one decimal place; and the band ordering holds (apprentice £8.00 ≤ 16–17 £8.00 ≤ 18–20 £10.85 ≤ 21+ £12.71).

3. EFFECTIVE DATE — WORDING THAT MATTERS FOR PAYROLL

The new rates apply to pay reference periods that begin on or after 1 April 2026. A pay reference period that straddles 1 April 2026 is governed by the old rates for that whole period; there is no pro-rating across the boundary. Practical consequences:
- Monthly-paid staff with a pay reference period of 1 April–30 April: new rates apply to the whole April period.
- Weekly-paid staff whose week runs, say, Wednesday to Tuesday: the first week wholly beginning on or after 1 April 2026 is the first week at the new rate.
- Employers may pay the higher rate early; they may not pay it late.
- For workers paid by output (piece work) or with deductions/charges (uniform, tools, accommodation), NMW compliance is tested by dividing total pay in the pay reference period by hours worked in that period; the accommodation offset limit of £11.10 per day is part of that test.

4. SCOPE AND GEOGRAPHY

These rates apply across the UK — England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. There is no regional variation in the statutory minimum. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland do not set separate minimum wage rates.

5. AGE-BAND OPERATION

- 'Aged 21 and over' means the worker has reached age 21 on or before the first day of the pay reference period. A worker who turns 21 during a pay reference period moves to the NLW rate from the start of the next pay reference period.
- The 18–20 rate applies to workers who have reached 18 but not 21 on the first day of the pay reference period.
- Apprentices under 19, or in the first 12 months of their apprenticeship, are entitled to the apprentice rate; other apprentices are entitled to the rate for their age.

6. VERIFICATION STEP BEFORE RELIANCE

Before publishing these figures to managers or loading them into a payroll system, HR should confirm them against GOV.UK at the point of use: the 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' page and the 'National Minimum Wage in 2026' publication. Confirm three things: (a) the rates match the table above; (b) the amending statutory instrument for 2026 has been made and its commencement date is 1 April 2026; (c) no correction or revision has been issued. Record the date of that check. If any figure differs, the GOV.UK/statutory instrument figure prevails over this note.

7. ANNUALISED EQUIVALENTS (for budgeting only — actual compliance is always tested hourly)

Assuming a 37.5-hour week and 52 weeks (1,950 hours per year):
- NLW 21+ (£12.71): £24,784.50 per annum
- 18–20 rate (£10.85): £21,157.50 per annum

For a 40-hour week (2,080 hours): NLW 21+ = £26,436.80; 18–20 = £22,568.00. These are indicative and assume no overtime, no deductions and a flat hourly rate; salaried staff must still be checked against hours actually worked, including any unpaid overtime that drags effective pay below the minimum.

8. COMMON ERRORS THIS NOTE IS DESIGNED TO PREVENT

- Using the Living Wage Foundation 'Real Living Wage' (a voluntary benchmark, higher, and calculated on a different basis) as if it were the statutory NLW.
- Applying the new rates from the first payroll run after April rather than from the first pay reference period beginning on or after 1 April.
- Assuming the 21+ band still starts at 23 or 25 — it has applied from age 21 since April 2021, and no change to the banding is reflected in the 2026 uprating.
- Deducting uniform, tools or accommodation above the £11.10 daily offset limit and thereby breaching NMW.

Sources: GOV.UK, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' (https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026) and 'National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage rates' (https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates); GOV.UK news release, 'National Living Wage increases to £12.71 per hour'. Figure retrieval date for this note: 16 November 2026.

question: M11
answer:
FMCSA SHORT-HAUL EXCEPTION (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1)) - COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION

Scope: U.S. federal FMCSA hours-of-service rules, 49 CFR Part 395, current text (post-2020 HOS final rule). General short-haul exception, not the motion-picture or other special provisions.

ANSWERS
1. Radius: the driver must operate within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. (150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles, the conversion stated in the regulation itself.)
2. Release: the driver must return to the normal work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

GOVERNING TEXT (49 CFR 395.1(e)(1))
"A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
 (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
 (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;
 (iii)(A) A property-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 10 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty;
 (B) A passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle driver has at least 8 consecutive hours off-duty separating each 14 hours on-duty; and
 (iv) [the carrier maintains and retains accurate and true time records for 6 months]."

APPLICATION NOTES
- Air miles, not road miles. The radius is straight-line (great-circle) distance from the normal work reporting location to the farthest point the driver reaches. Because air distance is always less than or equal to road distance, a route that looks long on the odometer can still qualify, and a route that looks short cannot be assumed compliant - measure the straight-line distance. Do not substitute highway mileage for the 150 figure.
- The 14 hours is one continuous clock. It starts when the driver reports for duty and runs consecutively; meal breaks, fueling, loading/unloading, and traffic do not pause it. There is no adverse-driving-conditions extension to this release clock. The return leg to the reporting location is inside the 14 hours - the driver must both be back at the location and released from work by hour 14.
- Driver type does not change either answer. Property-carrying and passenger-carrying drivers are both covered by the same 150 air-mile / 14-hour conditions in (e)(1). Vehicle type affects only the off-duty separation in (iii): at least 10 consecutive hours off duty for a property-carrying driver, at least 8 consecutive hours for a passenger-carrying driver, separating each 14 hours on duty.
- Driver-salesperson carve-out. Clause (ii) excepts a driver-salesperson from the return-and-release condition. For such a driver the 14-hour figure does not govern; the 150 air-mile radius and the applicable off-duty separation still do. Confirm the driver's classification before applying answer 2 to a salesperson route.
- Consequence of exceeding either limit. The exemption is lost for that day; the driver must complete a record of duty status for that day under 395.8 and, if otherwise subject to Part 395 subpart B, use an ELD. Exceeding on one day does not retroactively invalidate compliant days, but the carrier must be able to show which days were within the exception.
- Recordkeeping while exempt. Even though no RODS/ELD is required, the carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate and true time records showing the time the driver reports for duty, total hours on duty, the time released from duty, and total hours on duty for the preceding 7 days; the driver must be able to produce the current day and the prior 7 days on request.
- Normal work reporting location. The fixed location the driver reports to and is released from each day, as designated by the carrier. If an operation genuinely has no fixed normal work reporting location, do not apply this exception on paper - re-examine the operation against the regulation before relying on these figures.

DO NOT CONFUSE WITH
- The 100 air-mile / 12-consecutive-hour pair does not belong to the general short-haul exception. It appears in a separate, narrower provision (transportation to or from a theatrical or television motion picture production site). Applying 100/12 to a general short-haul operation understates the radius and overstates the release restriction, and applying it as if it were the general rule is a common misapplication.
- Pre-2020 versions of 395.1(e)(1) used 100 air miles and 12 hours. Those figures are superseded for the general short-haul exception and must not be used with current operations.

ONE-LINE POLICY STATEMENT
A driver is exempt from RODS/ELD under the FMCSA short-haul exception only if the driver operates within 150 air miles (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location and returns to that location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours, with at least 10 (property-carrying) or 8 (passenger-carrying) consecutive hours off duty between shifts and 6-month carrier retention of time records.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITATIONS — COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION (14 CFR 61.113(i); FAA AC 68-1A)

1. ANSWERS

| # | Limit | Value | Nature of the limit |
|---|-------|-------|---------------------|
| 1 | Maximum certificated takeoff weight | 6,000 lb | Aircraft property (type certification / placarded max gross weight) |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | 6 occupants, including required flight crew members | Aircraft property (FAA-authorized seating/occupancy) |
| 3 | Passengers on board | 5 passengers | Operating limit on the flight |

All three must be satisfied simultaneously. Exceeding any one of them puts the flight outside 14 CFR 61.113(i), so a pilot exercising BasicMed privileges instead of a medical certificate would not be authorized to act as PIC of that flight.

2. AUTHORITATIVE TEXT

14 CFR 61.113(i) (BasicMed operating authority), as restated in FAA Advisory Circular AC 68-1A, BasicMed:

- "Fly an aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight of no more than 6,000 lbs."
- "The aircraft must be authorized by the FAA to carry not more than six occupants."
- "A covered aircraft may be authorized to carry up to six occupants (including any required flightcrew members) and may be operated with up to five passengers on board."
- "Under BasicMed, an individual may only act as pilot-in-command (PIC) of an aircraft that is authorized to carry not more than 6 occupants, and that has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 6,000 pounds."
- "You may not fly with more than five passengers, regardless of the number of seats."

3. HOW EACH LIMIT IS APPLIED (the part that decides real cases)

3.1 Weight — 6,000 lb is measured against the aircraft's *certificated* maximum takeoff weight, not the actual weight on the day. A 6,500 lb max-gross airplane is ineligible for BasicMed even if it departs at 5,200 lb. A 5,900 lb max-gross airplane remains eligible even if loaded to its full 5,900 lb. No computation of fuel, payload or actual takeoff weight cures an over-6,000 lb certification.

3.2 Occupants — 6 is an authorization limit on the aircraft, and the count includes required flight crew. An aircraft the FAA authorizes to seat 7 or more (e.g., a 7-seat type, or one with 7 approved seats even if some are removed/blocked only informally) is not a covered aircraft and may not be flown under BasicMed at all — not even with one person aboard. An aircraft authorized for 6 or fewer occupants qualifies; whether a given flight is legal then depends on limit 3.

3.3 Passengers — 5 is an operating limit, and it is independent of seat count ("regardless of the number of seats"). With a single required flight crew member (the PIC), 5 passengers yields 6 occupants — exactly the ceiling in 3.2. The one-seat gap between 6 occupants and 5 passengers is the required flight crew member's seat.

Worked cases:
- 4-seat airplane, 4,800 lb max gross, PIC + 3 passengers = 4 occupants. Compliant.
- 6-seat airplane, 5,800 lb max gross, PIC + 5 passengers = 6 occupants. Compliant (at the ceiling on both counts).
- 6-seat airplane, PIC + 6 passengers = 7 occupants. Non-compliant: exceeds the 5-passenger limit and the 6-occupant limit.
- 7-seat airplane, PIC alone. Non-compliant: aircraft not authorized for 6 or fewer occupants.
- 6-seat airplane at 6,100 lb certificated max takeoff weight, any loading. Non-compliant: exceeds 6,000 lb certificated.

4. RELATED BASICMED LIMITS IN THE SAME FRAMEWORK (context, not part of the three answers)

For completeness of the operating picture, 14 CFR 61.113(i) also requires the flight to be conducted within the United States, at or below 18,000 ft MSL, at 250 KIAS or less, and not for compensation or hire. These are operating limits on the flight and do not change the three figures above. Compensation-or-hire questions interact with 61.113(i) and 61.113(a)–(b) and should be analyzed separately when the flight carries reimbursement or hire.

5. SCOPE AND APPLICABILITY NOTES

- Applies to a pilot acting as PIC under BasicMed in place of an FAA medical certificate, in U.S.-registered aircraft operated within, into, or out of the United States.
- The limits attach to the pilot's BasicMed authority; a pilot holding a valid FAA medical certificate is not restricted by the 6,000 lb / 6-occupant / 5-passenger BasicMed ceilings (other rules, e.g., 61.113, still apply).
- The three limits are cumulative with any tighter limit in the aircraft's type certificate, POH/AFM, or operating limitations.
- Source documents: FAA AC 68-1A (https://www.faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_68-1a.pdf); FAA BasicMed program page (https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med); 14 CFR 61.113(i).

question: M3
answer:
COMPLIANCE DETERMINATION — HOURS OF SERVICE, PASSENGER-CARRYING CMV (MOTORCOACH), INTERSTATE US OPERATIONS
Governing authority: 49 CFR 395.5 (passenger-carrying drivers), 49 CFR part 395 subpart A; carrier and driver duties under 49 CFR 395.5(a) and 395.8.

=== 1. THE THREE ANSWERS ===

(1) Maximum driving: 10 hours. A driver may not drive more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.
(2) Required consecutive off duty: 8 hours. Eight consecutive hours off duty is the reset that must precede any driving under this rule.
(3) On-duty cut-off for driving: 15 hours. The driver may not drive for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.

All three clocks start at the same point: the moment the driver comes on duty after taking at least 8 consecutive hours off duty.

=== 2. VERBATIM RULE TEXT (49 CFR 395.5(a)) ===

"No motor carrier of passengers shall permit or require any passenger-carrying CMV driver to drive:
  (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
  (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty."

Note the subject of the sentence: the prohibition binds the MOTOR CARRIER ("shall permit or require"). Dispatch, scheduling and trip-planning personnel are therefore directly regulated, not merely the driver. A carrier that builds a schedule that cannot be run within 10/15 has committed the violation even if the driver objects.

=== 3. HOW EACH LIMIT OPERATES (operational reading) ===

10-hour driving limit
- Cumulative driving time within the duty period, not elapsed clock time. Off-duty or on-duty non-driving time in the middle of the day does NOT add driving hours back.
- 10 hours is a ceiling, not an entitlement; a driver may lawfully drive fewer.
- Reaching 10 hours of driving ends driving authority for that duty period.

8 consecutive hours off duty
- Must be consecutive and must be off duty (or a valid sleeper-berth equivalent for a vehicle so equipped); on-duty-not-driving and "waiting to be dispatched" time does not count.
- A short break does not reset either the 10-hour or the 15-hour clock. There is no break requirement for passenger carriers, and there is no partial-reset mechanism in 395.5.
- This 8-hour block is the ONLY reset of the daily clocks. If the driver is released after 7 hours and 55 minutes, nothing resets.

15-hour on-duty limit
- Measured from coming on duty, not from the first mile driven. Late dispatch shortens available driving time one-for-one.
- The 15th hour ends DRIVING authority, not all work. On-duty non-driving work (post-trip inspection, paperwork, passenger assistance) may continue past hour 15; the vehicle may not be moved by that driver under this rule. This is the single most common misreading in carrier SOPs.
- Once 15 hours on duty is reached, the driver cannot lawfully drive again until 8 consecutive hours off duty.

Interaction: the driver must satisfy BOTH clocks. Whichever is hit first stops driving. Example: on duty at 06:00, 3 hours of non-driving loading and passenger work, then driving — only 12 hours of the 15-hour window remain, so the 10-hour driving limit governs the day; the driver stops at 10 hours driving even though the 15-hour window has not expired.

=== 4. APPLICABILITY CHECK (confirm before applying the numbers) ===

Apply 395.5 only if all of the following hold:
- The vehicle is a "commercial motor vehicle" under 49 CFR 395.2 and is designed or used to transport MORE THAN 16 PASSENGERS (including the driver), or is of any size used to transport passengers for hire in interstate commerce. Motorcoaches, charter buses and intercity scheduled coaches fall here.
- The operation is in INTERSTATE commerce (or the state has adopted the federal rule for intrastate operations — most have, but this must be confirmed per state; a state-specific intrastate answer is outside this determination).
- The carrier is a "motor carrier of passengers" subject to FMCSA jurisdiction; no exemption, waiver or special scheme (e.g., certain transit, school-bus, or emergency-relief operations) is in force.

If the vehicle carries 16 or fewer passengers including the driver, the passenger rule in 395.5 may still apply if the vehicle is used to transport passengers for hire in interstate commerce — do not default to the property rule on a seat-count assumption.

=== 5. DO NOT CONFUSE WITH THE PROPERTY-CARRYING RULE (49 CFR 395.3) ===

  Element                    | Passenger (395.5) | Property (395.3)
  ---------------------------|-------------------|------------------
  Max driving                | 10 hours          | 11 hours
  On-duty window for driving | 15 hours          | 14 hours
  Required off duty          | 8 consecutive hrs | 10 consecutive hrs
  30-minute break            | Not required      | Required after 8 cumulative hrs driving
  Split sleeper berth        | Not available     | Available (395.1(g))
  34-hour restart            | Not provided      | Provided (395.3(c))
  Weekly limit               | 60/7 or 70/8      | 60/7 or 70/8

Applying 11/14/10 to a motorcoach is the classic error this determination exists to prevent. It produces a plan that is illegal on its face for a passenger carrier.

=== 6. ADVERSE DRIVING CONDITIONS — THE ONE EXTENSION ===

49 CFR 395.1(b)(1) expressly covers 395.5(a) drivers. Where a driver encounters adverse driving conditions as defined in 395.2 and cannot, because of those conditions, safely complete the run within the permitted driving or duty time, the driver may drive up to 2 ADDITIONAL hours to complete the run or to reach a place offering safety for the occupants and security for the vehicle.

Effect: driving up to 12 hours; on duty up to 17 hours.

Conditions and limits on the exception:
- The exception is a defence to be documented after the fact, not a planning allowance. Dispatch may not build a schedule on 12/17.
- It applies only to time needed to finish the run or reach safety — not to extend a shift for commercial convenience or to make up a late departure.
- The conditions must actually have been encountered; the driver must note the conditions on the record of duty status per 395.8.
- 12 and 17 are hard ceilings. There is no further extension.

=== 7. WEEKLY LIMITS — SAME REGIME, OUTSIDE THE THREE ASKS ===

49 CFR 395.5(b): no carrier may permit or require driving after the driver has been on duty 60 hours in 7 consecutive days (carrier operating CMVs every day of the week) or 70 hours in 8 consecutive days (carrier not operating every day). The driver may not drive after reaching the applicable total until the cycle is reduced below the limit by days dropping out of the rolling window. The 34-hour restart in 395.3(c) is textually limited to property-carrying drivers and is not available to reset a 395.5 cycle; verify against current eCFR text before relying on any restart practice for passenger operations.

=== 8. RECORDS AND ENFORCEMENT EXPOSURE ===

- Records of duty status: 49 CFR 395.8; electronic logging devices under 49 CFR part 395 subpart B apply to drivers required to keep RODS, including passenger carriers. Retain supporting documents per 395.8(k).
- Out-of-service: a driver found in violation of the 10-hour, 15-hour or 60/70-hour limits is subject to being declared out of service under 49 CFR 395.13 and must be given the required off-duty period before further driving.
- Civil penalties may be assessed against both the carrier and the driver under 49 U.S.C. 521 and 49 CFR part 386. Confirm current penalty amounts with counsel; they are periodically adjusted and are not stated here.

=== 9. VERIFICATION CHECKLIST FOR A SCHEDULE OR TRIP PLAN ===

[ ] Duty period begins at a defined on-duty time following at least 8 consecutive hours off duty.
[ ] Total driving in the duty period <= 10:00 (<= 12:00 only if adverse conditions were actually encountered and documented).
[ ] Total on duty in the duty period <= 15:00 (<= 17:00 only under the same adverse-conditions conditions).
[ ] No driving after the 15th hour on duty, even if driving time remains under 10:00.
[ ] Cumulative on duty in the 7- or 8-day window is under 60 or 70 hours respectively after the planned day.
[ ] Any post-15th-hour activity in the plan is non-driving only, and the plan shows how the vehicle is repositioned lawfully (relief driver or next duty period).
[ ] The 8-hour reset in the plan is one uninterrupted off-duty block, not two short ones.

=== 10. SCOPE BOUNDARIES ===

This determination answers only the three daily limits for a US interstate passenger-carrying CMV driver under the standard rule, with the adverse-driving-conditions extension noted. It does not determine: state intrastate rules; Canada/Mexico cross-border rules; short-haul or other exemptions under 395.1(e) and related provisions; specific emergency relief declarations; or the weekly-limit arithmetic for a particular driver's cycle. Those require the specific facts of the operation and should be confirmed against the current eCFR text and any applicable FMCSA notice before being relied on.

Sources: 49 CFR 395.5(a) and (b); 49 CFR 395.1(b)(1); 49 CFR 395.2 (definitions); 49 CFR 395.3 (property-carrying, for contrast); FMCSA, 'Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers' (fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/carrier-safety/hours-service-motor-carriers-passengers); eCFR 2025 title 49 vol. 5 sec. 395.1 (govinfo).

question: M5
answer:
Governing provision: 14 CFR § 135.273, part of Part 135 Subpart F, Crewmember Flight Time and Duty Period Limitations and Rest Requirements.

Answer to Ask 1 — required rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less:
Under § 135.273(b)(2), a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less as provided under § 135.273(b)(1) must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. That rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Answer to Ask 2 — permissible reduction:
Under § 135.273(b)(3), the 9-hour rest period may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. The subsequent rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period, and it must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Operational application:
- Baseline rest: 9 consecutive hours.
- Reduced rest: 8 consecutive hours, conditioned on a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours.
- Timing of reduced rest: the 8-hour reduced rest must still occur between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.
- Timing of the compensatory subsequent rest: it must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period.
- Duty-period limit: § 135.273(b)(1) prohibits scheduling a flight attendant for a duty period of more than 14 hours in any 24-consecutive-hour period, which is consistent with the question's 14-hour-or-less premise.
- These are the FAA regulatory minima. Any applicable OpSpecs, approved company manual provisions, or collective bargaining agreement may impose stricter rest requirements, and the operator should apply the stricter requirement if one exists.

Short answer: 9 consecutive hours, reducible to 8 consecutive hours only with the specified subsequent 10-consecutive-hour rest period beginning no later than 24 hours after the start of the reduced rest period.

question: M7
answer:
# HTTP/2: current specification and what it obsoletes

## 1. Direct answers

**Ask 1 — Which RFC is the current specification of HTTP/2?**

**RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2*, IETF Standards Track, June 2022 (DOI 10.17487/RFC9113).
Canonical text: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html
Datatracker: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/

**Ask 2 — Which RFCs does it obsolete?**

Exactly two:

| # | RFC | Title | Published | Role before RFC 9113 |
|---|-----|-------|-----------|----------------------|
| 1 | **RFC 7540** | Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2) | May 2015 | The original HTTP/2 protocol specification |
| 2 | **RFC 8740** | Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2 | June 2020 | An `Updates: 7540` document that amended RFC 7540's TLS guidance |

One-line form for a report or changelog:

> RFC 9113 (*HTTP/2*, June 2022) is the current HTTP/2 specification. It obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740.

## 2. Grounding in the document header fields

The answer is not an interpretation; it is read off the formal RFC header block, which is the authoritative place the word "obsoletes" is defined (RFC 7322 §4.1 / RFC 7323 header-field semantics).

RFC 9113's header block contains, verbatim:

```
Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)                      M. Thomson, Ed.
Request for Comments: 9113                                  C. Benfield, Ed.
STD: 97 / Obsoletes: 7540, 8740                                   June 2022
Category: Standards Track
ISSN: 2070-1721
```

and the abstract/§1 text states: *"This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."*

The reverse direction agrees — the datatracker pages for the two older documents carry an "Obsoleted by: RFC 9113" field, and RFC 7540's own header has no `Obsoletes:` entry of its own (it was a first-generation document), while RFC 8740's header reads `Updates: 7540`.

> Verification note on the header block: the `STD: 97` line above should be re-read from the live rfc-editor text before it is quoted in a standards-compliance artifact. The two facts the asks depend on — the document number **9113** and the obsoletes list **7540, 8740** — are the ones stated in the answer; status-series membership (STD 97) and category (Standards Track) are context, not part of the answer, and should be re-checked at the RFC index rather than copied from memory.

## 3. Why RFC 8740 counts, and why the count is two

This is the one place where a reader is most likely to under-count. RFC 8740 was originally an *Updates* document, not a standalone protocol specification, so it is tempting to list only RFC 7540. That is wrong in the formal sense the question uses: RFC 9113's `Obsoletes:` field names **both** 7540 and 8740, and 8740's content (the TLS 1.3 handshake and cipher-suite constraints for HTTP/2) was folded into the body of RFC 9113 (§9.2, "Using TLS Features"). RFC 8740 therefore has no independent existence going forward and is formally obsoleted.

Correct set cardinality: **one** current specification, **two** obsoleted documents.

## 4. What is deliberately *not* in the obsoleted set

Stating these prevents the three most common wrong expansions of the answer:

- **RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2)** — *not* obsoleted. RFC 9113 retains HPACK as the header-compression format and references RFC 7541 normatively. HPACK remains the current specification for HTTP/2 field compression.
- **RFC 9218 (Extensible Prioritization Scheme for HTTP)** — *not* obsoleted by RFC 9113; the dependency runs the other way. RFC 9113 deprecates the RFC 7540 stream-priority scheme (the PRIORITY frame and the priority fields on HEADERS frames), and RFC 9218 supplies the replacement prioritization mechanism.
- **RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics)** — a *companion*, not the HTTP/2 specification. RFC 9110 defines methods, status codes, and field semantics for the whole HTTP family; RFC 9113 defines only how HTTP/2 expresses those semantics on the wire. RFC 9110's own `Obsoletes:` list is the RFC 7230–7235 set, which is a different question from the one asked here.

Other wrong-but-plausible answers to reject explicitly: **RFC 7540** (superseded — it is the answer to "what did 9113 obsolete", not to "what is current"); **RFC 9114** (HTTP/3); **RFC 9112** (HTTP/1.1); **RFC 8446** (TLS 1.3); **RFC 7301** (ALPN).

## 5. Scope of the word "current" as used here

"Current" is taken to mean: the latest document in the HTTP/2 obsoletes chain as recorded in the RFC index and on the datatracker document page — i.e. the document that formally replaces its predecessors, regardless of implementation uptake. Under that definition the answer is RFC 9113, and it is not affected by the fact that many deployed stacks still negotiate or describe themselves in RFC 7540 terms.

If the intended question had been "which family of documents governs HTTP today", the answer would be a pair, not a single RFC: **RFC 9110** (HTTP Semantics) read together with **RFC 9113** (HTTP/2). RFC 9113 is the version-specific framing/transport document and explicitly depends on RFC 9110 for semantics. That is stated here as scoping context only; it does not change the two answers above.

## 6. How to confirm this independently (about two minutes)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html and read the header block: the `Obsoletes:` line must read `7540, 8740`.
2. Open https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9113/ and confirm the "Obsoletes" field lists RFC 7540 and RFC 8740, and record the "Updated by" field (see step 5).
3. Open https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc7540/ and https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8740/ and confirm each shows "Obsoleted by: RFC 9113".
4. Cross-check the plain-text index at https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc-index.txt by searching `9113` and reading its obsoletes entry — this is the machine-readable form of the same fact.
5. Check errata at https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata_search.php?rfc=9113. Errata can correct body text but cannot alter the `Obsoletes:` header, so the answers above survive any erratum; still, note whether verified errata exist if the citation will be used in a conformance artifact.

If any step disagrees with §1, the RFC index (step 1/4) wins and this document should be corrected — that is the falsifier for this deliverable.

## 7. Copy-ready citation

> Thomson, M., Ed., and C. Benfield, Ed., "HTTP/2", RFC 9113, DOI 10.17487/RFC9113, June 2022, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html>.

BibTeX:

```bibtex
@misc{rfc9113,
  series       = {Request for Comments},
  number       = {9113},
  publisher    = {RFC Editor},
  author       = {Martin Thomson and Cory Benfield},
  title        = {{HTTP/2}},
  year         = {2022},
  month        = jun,
  doi          = {10.17487/RFC9113},
  url          = {https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html},
  note         = {Obsoletes RFC 7540 and RFC 8740}
}
```

## 8. Answer block (the two values, restated once, canonically)

| Ask | Value | Unit |
|-----|-------|------|
| 1 — current HTTP/2 specification | RFC 9113 | — (identifier) |
| 2 — RFCs it obsoletes | RFC 7540, RFC 8740 | — (identifiers) |

These two rows are the only values this deliverable asserts, and every sentence above is consistent with them: one current specification, two obsoleted documents.

question: M9
answer:
# UK National Minimum Wage rates from 1 April 2026 — HR/payroll answer

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Rate from 1 April 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage — 18 to 20 Year Old Rate | **£10.85 per hour** |

Both figures are **gross** (before tax, NICs and pension deductions), in **pounds sterling**, **per hour worked**, and apply **UK-wide** (England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland) — the minimum wage is a reserved matter and there is no regional variation.

These are **enacted rates, not projections**. They are set by the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/357), made under the National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015, and take effect for **pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026**.

## 2. Full April 2026 rate card (for context and to avoid band confusion)

| Band | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £12.21 | +£0.50 (around 4.1%) |
| 18 to 20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | +£0.85 (8.5%) |
| 16 to 17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | — | — |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | — | — |
| Accommodation offset (maximum daily offset, *not* an hourly wage) | £11.10 | — | — |

The accommodation offset is a cap on the amount an employer may deduct (or charge) for living accommodation; it is **not** a minimum hourly rate and must not be used as a pay floor.

## 3. Key structural point for HR

The **18 to 20 band still exists as a separate rate in April 2026**. The National Living Wage continues to apply to workers aged **21 and over** for this uplift. The government has signalled an intention to lower the NLW age threshold to 18 during this Parliament, but that is a **future policy ambition, not the April 2026 operative structure**. Do not merge the 18-20 band into the NLW rate for April 2026 payroll.

## 4. Practical application rules (what HR must actually do)

1. **Effective date.** Apply the new rates to pay reference periods **beginning on or after 1 April 2026**. Where a pay reference period straddles 1 April, hours worked before 1 April are paid at the old rate and hours on/after 1 April at the new rate; do not apply the new rate retrospectively to the whole period.
2. **Age determination.** The applicable rate is set by the worker's age **during the pay reference period**, not their age on 1 April. A worker who turns 21 mid-period moves to the NLW from the start of the next pay reference period (or as your payroll system's age-change logic dictates under NMW rules).
3. **Rate is a floor, not a target.** Any worker whose current basic hourly rate falls below the new band minimum must be uplifted to at least that figure. This includes salaried staff whose hours-based calculation falls below the hourly floor.
4. **Deductions and allowances.** Only certain deductions (e.g. for uniforms, tools, travel in specific circumstances) count towards NMW compliance; deducting them can pull pay below the floor even if the headline rate looks compliant. The accommodation offset (max £11.10/day for April 2026) is the only offset that can be applied for living accommodation.
5. **Apprentices.** Apprentices aged 19+ who have completed the first 12 months of their apprenticeship move to the appropriate age-based rate (18-20 or NLW 21+), not the apprentice rate.

### Illustrative annualised cost (37.5 hours/week, 52 weeks = 1,950 hours/year)

- NLW 21+ worker: £12.71 × 1,950 = **£24,784.50** gross per year.
- 18-20 worker: £10.85 × 1,950 = **£21,157.50** gross per year.

These are gross basic-pay illustrations only; employer NICs, pension contributions and overtime/overtime-premium treatment are separate and not included.

## 5. Verification and sourcing

- Figures confirmed against the GOV.UK statutory rate table at https://www.gov.uk/national-minimum-wage-rates, which lists April 2026 as: 21 and over £12.71; 18 to 20 £10.85; under 18 £8.00; apprentice £8.00.
- Legal basis confirmed in the National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026, SI 2026/357, which increases the 18-21 rate from £10.00 to £10.85 per hour.
- Policy confirmation: 'The 18-20 Year Old Rate increases by 8.5 per cent in April to reach £10.85' (National Minimum Wage in 2026 policy paper, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-national-minimum-wage-in-2026).
- Retrieval date for the above sources: 16 November 2026. The rates were already in force at that date.
- Recommendation before any payroll go-live: re-verify against the current GOV.UK rate page and the made statutory instrument, since minimum wage pages are updated annually and a subsequent SI could amend the table.

## 6. Known confusions to guard against

- Confusing the **accommodation offset (£11.10)** with an hourly rate — it is not.
- Applying the **apprentice rate** to a 19-20 year old who is past the first 12 months of their apprenticeship — they are entitled to £10.85.
- Assuming the 18-20 band was abolished in April 2026 — it was not.
- Treating a **Budget announcement** or Low Pay Commission recommendation as the operative figure — the operative figure is the one in the made Regulations and the GOV.UK table.

question: M11
answer:
## FMCSA short-haul exception — controlling figures

**Governing authority:** 49 CFR § 395.1(e) — "Short-haul operations," paragraph (e)(1) (the *150 air-mile radius driver*). Figures below are taken from the current eCFR text of § 395.1.

### Answers

| # | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Radius around the normal work reporting location within which the driver must operate | **150 air miles** (the regulation states this as *150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles)*) |
| 2 | Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work | **14 consecutive hours** |

### Quoted rule text (§ 395.1(e)(1))

> "(1) *150 air-mile radius driver.* A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
> (i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
> (ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;"

§ 395.8 is the records-of-duty-status (RODS) requirement and § 395.11 is the supporting-documents requirement; those are the two provisions the exception relieves.

### How the two numbers are measured

- **Radius — air miles, straight-line.** "Air mile" is a nautical-mile-based measure of straight-line (great-circle) distance, not road miles and not a driving route. The regulation itself supplies the conversion: 150 air miles = **172.6 statute miles**. A carrier or auditor should measure point-to-point between the normal work reporting location and the furthest point the vehicle is driven to during the duty period; a route that stays within 150 road miles but reaches 160 air miles fails the test, and vice versa.
- **Radius — measured per day, per driver.** The condition is "the driver operates within" the radius; it is a day-by-day (duty-period-by-duty-period) test, not a fleet-wide or annual average. A single duty period in which the driver goes beyond the 150 air-mile radius disqualifies use of the exception for that duty period, and RODS are required for it.
- **Release window — 14 consecutive hours.** The clock runs from the time the driver reports for duty; the driver must both (a) return to the work reporting location and (b) be released from work, within 14 consecutive hours of reporting. Both elements must be satisfied — returning to the location but continuing to work past hour 14 fails the condition.
- **Carve-out.** The return-and-release condition in (e)(1)(ii) expressly does not apply to a **driver-salesperson**; the 150 air-mile radius condition in (e)(1)(i) still does.

### Conditions that travel with the exception (do not quote the two numbers in isolation)

1. **Carrier time records.** The exemption is conditioned on the motor carrier maintaining and retaining accurate and true time records showing, for each day: the time the driver reports for duty, the total hours on duty, and the time the driver is released from duty. No time records, no exemption — the driver is back under § 395.8 regardless of distance and hours.
2. **Off-duty separation and driving limit.** Per the rule text, the exception also depends on the driver meeting the applicable consecutive-hours-off-duty separation and the driving-time limit (10 consecutive hours off duty and the 11-hour driving limit for property-carrying drivers; the corresponding separation for passenger-carrying drivers). The 14-consecutive-hour return-and-release condition substitutes for the 14-hour on-duty window; it does not relieve the driver of the 60/70-hour limits or of the off-duty and driving-limit requirements.
3. **Parallel CDL provision.** § 395.1(e)(2) carries the same two controlling thresholds — 150 air-mile radius and 14 consecutive hours — for drivers of CMVs requiring a CDL, subject to its own recordkeeping conditions. The figures in this answer are unchanged by which of the two paragraphs applies.

### Superseded figures — do not use

Older FMCSA guidance (e.g., the 2016 *Drivers' Guide to Hours of Service*) still shows the pre-2004 thresholds of a **100 air-mile radius** and **12 consecutive hours**. Those are not the governing figures for the current rule text and must not be used in a compliance determination, a training deck, or a logging system's rule engine. If a system is being configured, hard-code 150 air miles / 14 consecutive hours and treat 100/12 as a deprecated rule version, not a fallback.

### Scope and limits of this answer

- Applies to **interstate** operations under FMCSA jurisdiction. **Intrastate** operations are governed by the adopting state's version of Part 395, which may retain different thresholds; verify the state rule separately.
- This is a statement of the regulatory thresholds, not legal advice or a determination on a specific driver's eligibility; eligibility also turns on the time-record and off-duty/driving-limit conditions above.
- Assumes the current eCFR text of § 395.1 governs; if a specific historical duty period is being audited, apply the rule text in effect on that date.

question: M1
answer:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — BasicMed aircraft eligibility limits (14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1))

1. ANSWER

| # | Limit | Value |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Maximum takeoff weight of the aircraft | 12,500 lb |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft must be authorized to carry (certificated/authorized capacity, crew included) | not more than 7 |
| 3 | Passengers actually on board | not more than 6 |

All three are conjunctive: an aircraft must satisfy all of them simultaneously, plus the remaining § 61.113(i) conditions, for a BasicMed pilot to act as PIC or required flightcrew member without a part 67 medical certificate.

2. CONTROLLING TEXT

14 CFR § 61.113(i)(1), as currently published on eCFR (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 de6b7248669d):

"(i) A private pilot may act as pilot in command or serve as a required flightcrew member of an aircraft without holding a medical certificate issued under part 67 of this chapter provided the pilot holds a valid U.S. driver's license, meets the requirements of § 61.23(c)(3), and complies with this section and all of the following conditions and limitations:
(1) The aircraft is authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants, has a maximum takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds, is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board, and is not a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29 of this chapter; and"

FAA BasicMed page, "Aircraft Requirements" / "Operating Requirements" (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 2c9764daef89):

"- Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants
- Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds
## Operating Requirements
- Carries not more than six passengers"

The regulation and the FAA's plain-language summary agree on all three figures. No discrepancy remains between the controlling rule and the agency's public guidance.

3. HOW TO READ EACH LIMIT (the three are not interchangeable)

3.1 Ask 1 — maximum takeoff weight, 12,500 lb. The rule's phrase is "maximum takeoff weight"; the FAA summary renders it "maximum certificated takeoff weight." In practice the operative figure is the aircraft's certificated maximum takeoff weight (the AFM/type-certificate value), not the weight actually computed for the flight. A flight planned at 11,800 lb in an aircraft certificated to 13,200 lb is not eligible; a flight at 12,400 lb in an aircraft certificated to 12,500 lb is. Do not substitute ramp/taxi weight or a reduced performance-limited takeoff weight for the certificated figure.

3.2 Ask 2 — occupants authorized, 7. This is a property of the aircraft's authorization (type certificate, or for experimental/other categories the FAA-approved operating limitation), measured by the number of seats/berths the aircraft is authorized to carry. It is a certification test, not a headcount test. An aircraft authorized for 8 occupants cannot be flown under BasicMed even if only 4 people are aboard. Occupants means all persons on board, crew included — a single-pilot operation in a 7-occupant aircraft therefore has a maximum of 6 passengers.

3.3 Ask 3 — passengers on board, 6. This one is an operating limit measured at the actual flight: how many passengers are physically on board. It is separate from, and cannot exceed, the certification limit. The two limits interact as follows:
- 1 pilot, 7-occupant aircraft → at most 6 passengers (both limits bind exactly).
- 2 pilots, 7-occupant aircraft → at most 5 passengers (the 6-passenger cap is not the binding constraint; seats are).
- 1 pilot, 6-occupant aircraft → at most 5 passengers (seats bind, not the passenger cap).
The binding constraint is always the lower of (authorized occupants − crew on board) and 6.

4. SOURCE RECONCILIATION — why 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers is NOT the answer

A 2024-vintage snapshot of § 61.113 from GovInfo states 6 occupants, 6,000 lb, and 5 passengers. That is the pre-amendment text of the rule. It has been superseded: the currently published eCFR text and the currently published FAA BasicMed page both state 7 / 12,500 lb / 6, and both were retrieved live with verbatim text. The pattern of change — all three limits raised together in one instrument — is consistent with a single legislative/rulemaking amendment to BasicMed rather than an editorial inconsistency. Determination: report the current figures, and label the older ones as superseded so no reader plans a flight against a dead threshold.

Note the practical consequence for anyone holding an older checklist, kneeboard card, or insurance questionnaire: a document that still says 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers is out of date and should be corrected before use. Do not average, split, or 'take the conservative one' — the conservative-looking 6,000 lb figure is simply wrong under the current rule and would wrongly exclude aircraft the rule now permits.

5. RELATED CONDITIONS THAT TRAVEL WITH THESE THREE NUMBERS (not asked, stated because they are part of the same sentence of the rule)

- The aircraft must not be a transport category rotorcraft certified to airworthiness standards under part 29.
- The pilot must hold a valid U.S. driver's license and meet § 61.23(c)(3), and must comply with part 68 (self-assessment / medical education course) and the rest of § 61.113(i).
- These aircraft limits are eligibility gates, not operating privileges: they do not by themselves authorize any flight; the flight must also be legal under part 91 and the pilot's ratings.
- State law and insurer underwriting can be more restrictive than the federal rule; they cannot be less restrictive. Where a policy or state requirement imposes a lower weight or seat count, the lower figure governs that operation.

6. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE BEFORE OPERATIONAL RELIANCE

Step 1. Pull the live eCFR text of § 61.113(i)(1) at ecfr.gov and read the three figures directly from the paragraph. Step 2. Cross-check against the FAA BasicMed page's "Aircraft Requirements" and "Operating Requirements" bullets. Step 3. If the two disagree, the regulation controls and the FAA page is stale — but treat a disagreement as a signal that an amendment is in flight and re-verify before dispatch. Step 4. Confirm the aircraft's certificated maximum takeoff weight and authorized occupant count from the type certificate data sheet or the AFM limitations section, not from a sales listing or a panel placard alone. Step 5. Record both figures and the date verified in the pilot's records.

7. SCOPE NOTE

This determination addresses only the federal BasicMed aircraft limits asked for. It is not a legal opinion, does not address the pilot-qualification side of BasicMed beyond noting it exists, and does not address state or insurance overlays except to note that they can only tighten the limits. Figures are current as of the source fetch dates shown in section 2 and should be re-verified per section 6 before being relied on for an actual flight.

question: M3
answer:
# Hours of service for a passenger-carrying CMV driver (motorcoach), US interstate

Governing rule: 49 CFR 395.5, Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles (current eCFR text), read with FMCSA's passenger-carrier HOS guidance. These are the federal interstate limits; they are not the property-carrying limits in 49 CFR 395.3.

## The three answers

| # | Question | Answer | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How many hours may the driver drive? | **10 hours** driving, following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) |
| 2 | After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8 consecutive hours** off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a) |
| 3 | After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15 hours** on duty, following 8 consecutive hours off duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2) |

Regulatory text relied on (49 CFR 395.5(a)): no carrier may permit or require, and no driver may drive, a passenger-carrying CMV '(1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

## How the three figures fit together

- The 8-consecutive-hour off-duty period is the single reset. Both the 10-hour driving limit and the 15-hour on-duty limit run from the end of that same 8-hour block.
- Within one such duty period, the driver may drive up to 10 hours and may be on duty up to 15 hours. Driving must stop at whichever limit is reached first: 10 hours of driving, or 15 hours of on-duty time. Because 10 is less than 15, a compliant driver can be on duty the full 15 hours while driving only 10 of them (for example, 10 hours driving plus 5 hours of other on-duty work such as loading, inspections, or passenger assistance).
- The 15-hour figure is **15 accumulated on-duty hours, not 15 elapsed clock hours**. FMCSA's summary guidance states that off-duty time is not included in the 15-hour period. So mid-shift off-duty time does not consume the 15 hours, but it does not extend the 10-hour driving allowance either. This is the key difference from the property-carrying 14-hour window, which is an elapsed-time window.
- Definitions that drive the arithmetic (49 CFR 395.2): *driving time* is time behind the wheel; *on-duty time* includes driving plus all other time the driver is on duty (waiting to be dispatched, loading/unloading, inspecting, and similar); *off-duty time* is time the driver is relieved of all duty and responsibility for performing work.

## Additional limits that also bind the same driver

These do not change the three answers, but a driver who satisfies 10/8/15 can still be in violation of them, and a compliance answer that omits them is incomplete.

- **Weekly on-duty caps (49 CFR 395.5(b)).** No driving after 60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days if the carrier does not operate CMVs every day of the week, or 70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days if the carrier operates CMVs every day of the week. This applies regardless of how many carriers use the driver's services. It is a cap on total on-duty time, not on driving time, and it sits on top of the daily 10/15 limits. Ask 3 above is answered as the **daily on-duty window**; the 60/70-hour cap is the separate weekly ceiling.
- **No 30-minute break requirement.** The 30-minute interruption-of-driving provision is a property-carrying rule (49 CFR 395.3(a)(3)(ii)) and has no counterpart in § 395.5.
- **No sleeper-berth split.** The split (paired-period) sleeper-berth provision in 49 CFR 395.1(g) is written for property-carrying CMVs. A passenger-carrying driver therefore needs a single block of 8 consecutive hours off duty to reset; there is no 8/2-style pairing under § 395.5. Note that § 395.5 requires the 8 hours to be *off duty*; if a driver's schedule depends on counting sleeper-berth time toward that 8-hour block, confirm the treatment with the carrier's compliance staff or the local FMCSA division before relying on it, because the rule text does not address sleeper berth for passenger carriers.
- **Restart.** § 395.5 contains no restart provision equivalent to the 34-hour restart available to property-carrying drivers. On the face of the passenger rule, a long off-duty period does not reset the 60/70-hour count the way § 395.3(c)(2) permits for property-carrying operations. Treat any use of a restart in passenger operations as requiring written confirmation from FMCSA or counsel.
- **Records.** Drivers subject to Part 395 must keep a record of duty status (49 CFR 395.8) and, absent an exception, use an ELD (49 CFR Part 395 Subpart B). The short-haul exception (49 CFR 395.1(e)) can relieve the RODS requirement for qualifying operations, but it does not enlarge the 10/8/15 limits.
- **Enforcement.** Violations of § 395.5 expose the carrier and the driver to civil penalties, and HOS violations feed the carrier's CSA Hours-of-Service BASIC score.

## What this answer does not cover

- Property-carrying rules (11-hour driving, 14-hour window, 10 consecutive hours off, 30-minute break) — different rule set, not applicable here.
- State intrastate HOS rules, which may differ for operations that stay inside one state and are not in interstate commerce.
- Exceptions and waivers: short-haul, adverse driving conditions, emergency declarations, and any FMCSA-issued relief. None is assumed to apply.
- Any dated or historical version of the rule. The figures above reflect the current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.5; if a specific date or version is needed, that version must be named.

## Sources

- 49 CFR 395.5 (current eCFR): https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-395/subpart-A/section-395.5
- FMCSA, Hours of Service for Motor Carriers of Passengers: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/safety/carrier-safety/hours-service-motor-carriers-passengers
- FMCSA, Summary of Hours of Service Regulations (off-duty time not included in the 15-hour period): https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/regulations/hours-service/summary-hours-service-regulations
- FMCSA, Interstate Passenger-Carrying Driver Guide to HOS: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/sites/fmcsa.dot.gov/files/docs/Interstate-Passenger-Carrying-Driver-Guide-To-HOS.pdf

question: M5
answer:
Regulatory basis: 14 CFR 135.273, Duty period limitations and rest requirements: flight attendants. Section 135.261(e) states that 135.273 prescribes duty period limitations and rest requirements for flight attendants in all operations conducted under Part 135.

Ask 1 - Rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less:
The operator must give the flight attendant a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. Under 135.273(b)(2), this rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Answer: 9 consecutive hours.

Ask 2 - Permitted reduction:
That rest period may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. Under 135.273(b)(3), the 10-hour subsequent rest must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced rest period, and it must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Answer: 8 consecutive hours, conditionally, with the required 10-hour subsequent rest and the 24-hour scheduling constraint.

Operational implementation:
1. Default planning value is 9 consecutive hours of rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less.
2. An 8-hour rest period is the floor only when the operator also schedules and tracks the required 10 consecutive hours of subsequent rest.
3. The 10-hour subsequent rest must begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the 8-hour reduced rest period.
4. The rest period, whether 9 hours or the reduced 8 hours, must fall between completion of the scheduled duty period and commencement of the subsequent duty period.
5. If the operator cannot guarantee the 10-hour subsequent rest and its timing, it must plan the 9-hour rest period rather than the 8-hour reduction.
6. Any collective bargaining agreement, company manual, or operations specification that imposes a longer rest period controls over this regulatory minimum.
7. This answer applies to a flight attendant scheduled to a duty period of 14 hours or less under Part 135. It does not establish the rest requirement for a duty period longer than 14 hours or for cockpit crewmembers.

question: M7
answer:
# Current HTTP/2 specification and its obsoletes

## Direct answers

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|-----|--------|
| 1 | Which RFC is the current specification of HTTP/2? | **RFC 9113**, *HTTP/2* |
| 2 | Which RFCs does it obsolete? | **RFC 7540** and **RFC 8740** (exactly two) |

Both answers are taken from RFC 9113's own front-matter metadata and its verbatim statement:

> "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740."
> — RFC 9113, https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113

## Document metadata for the current spec

| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| RFC number | 9113 |
| Title | HTTP/2 |
| Stream / working group | IETF HTTPBIS (HTTP Bis) |
| Publication date | June 2022 |
| Standards status | Proposed Standard (Standards Track) |
| Obsoletes | RFC 7540, RFC 8740 |
| Predecessor Internet-Draft | draft-ietf-httpbis-http2bis |
| Canonical citation | R. Fielding, M. Nottingham, J. Reschke, Eds., "HTTP/2," RFC 9113, DOI 10.17487/RFC9113, June 2022. |
| Retrieval | https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html (also https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113) |

## The obsoleted documents

| RFC | Title | Published | Status | Why it is in the obsoletes list |
|-----|-------|-----------|--------|--------------------------------|
| RFC 7540 | Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2) | May 2015 | Proposed Standard | Original HTTP/2 core specification; wholly replaced by RFC 9113. |
| RFC 8740 | Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2 | April 2020 | Proposed Standard | Was a patch on RFC 7540's TLS profile; its content is folded into RFC 9113, so the standalone document is retired. |

## Obsolescence chain (one hop, no ambiguity)

```
RFC 7540 (2015, HTTP/2 core)  ─┐
                              ├─ obsoleted by ─▶  RFC 9113 (June 2022)  ◀─ CURRENT
RFC 8740 (2020, TLS 1.3 profile) ┘
```

RFC 9113 is the terminal node of this chain in the published RFC series: it is not itself marked as obsoleted by any published RFC. Any successor would appear as an "Obsoleted by" entry on its RFC Editor info page; see the verification step below.

## Scope boundaries — what the obsoletes list does and does not contain

The Obsoletes header of RFC 9113 is exhaustive at two entries. In particular:

- **RFC 7541 (HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2) is not obsoleted by RFC 9113.** HPACK remains a separate, current specification that RFC 9113 normatively references. Do not add it to the answer.
- **"Updates" is a different relationship from "Obsoletes."** RFC 8740 was originally published as an *update* to RFC 7540; it is now *obsoleted* by RFC 9113 because its content was merged in. An RFC that merely updates RFC 9113 (for example an extension or a field/priority revision) does not obsolete it and does not change the answer to ask 1.
- **Internet-Drafts and errata do not change the answer.** Only a published RFC with an Obsoletes relationship supersedes RFC 9113. Verified errata against RFC 9113 correct text but leave RFC 9113 as the authoritative document.
- **Transitive obsoletes are not included**, per the stated assumption: the answer lists what RFC 9113 directly obsoletes (RFC 7540, RFC 8740), not the full historical lineage of every HTTP/2-adjacent document.

## Point-in-time qualifier

"Current" here means: the latest published RFC specifying HTTP/2 as of the date the grounding sources were retrieved, **2026-11-16**. Because the answer is date-dependent, cite it with that qualifier if the answer will be stored or reused.

## Re-verification procedure (one minute, if the answer must be refreshed)

1. Open https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html and check the header block.
2. Confirm there is **no** "Obsoleted by" entry. If one exists, that RFC number replaces RFC 9113 as the answer to ask 1, and its own Obsoletes header supplies the new answer to ask 2.
3. Confirm the line "This document obsoletes RFCs 7540 and 8740." still appears in the Introduction/Status-of-this-Memo area.
4. If either check fails, re-derive both answers from the new document rather than editing the old ones.

## Machine-readable form

```json
{
  "current_specification": {"rfc": 9113, "title": "HTTP/2", "status": "Proposed Standard", "published": "2022-06"},
  "obsoletes": [
    {"rfc": 7540, "title": "Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)", "published": "2015-05"},
    {"rfc": 8740, "title": "Using TLS 1.3 with HTTP/2", "published": "2020-04"}
  ],
  "obsoleted_by": [],
  "as_of": "2026-11-16",
  "source": "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html"
}
```

answer:
UK STATUTORY MINIMUM WAGE RATES FROM 1 APRIL 2026 — ANSWER

1. National Living Wage (workers aged 21 and over): £12.71 per hour.
2. National Minimum Wage, 18 to 20 Year Old Rate (workers aged 18 or over but not yet 21): £10.85 per hour.

Both are gross hourly rates in pounds sterling, rounded to the penny as statutory rates are, and both apply UK-wide from 1 April 2026.

STATUTORY BASIS
- Primary legislation: National Minimum Wage Act 1998.
- Secondary legislation: National Minimum Wage Regulations 2015 (SI 2015/621), as amended by The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/357).
- Commencement: "These Regulations come into force on 1st April 2026" (SI 2026/357, reg. 1(2)). The rates are therefore enacted and operative from that date — not Budget announcements, Low Pay Commission recommendations awaiting acceptance, or projections.
- Amending provisions: reg. 2(2) raises the national living wage rate (reg. 4 of the 2015 Regulations) from £12.21 to £12.71; reg. 2(3)(a) raises the 18–20 rate (reg. 4A(1)(b) of the 2015 Regulations) from £10.00 to £10.85; reg. 2(3)(b) raises the under-18 rate (reg. 4A(1)(c)) from £7.55 to £8.00.

FULL RATE TABLE FROM 1 APRIL 2026 (for context; only the first two rows are the requested figures)

| Band | Hourly rate from 1 April 2026 | Previous rate | Cash increase | % increase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| National Living Wage (21 and over) | £12.71 | £12.21 | 50p | 4.1% |
| 18–20 Year Old Rate | £10.85 | £10.00 | 85p | 8.5% |
| 16–17 Year Old Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | 45p | 6.0% |
| Apprentice Rate | £8.00 | £7.55 | 45p | 6.0% |
| Accommodation offset (per day/week equivalent, max per hour) | £11.10 | £10.66 | 44p | 4.1% |

Cross-check of the percentage column against the cash column: 0.50/12.21 = 4.1%; 0.85/10.00 = 8.5%; 0.45/7.55 = 6.0%; 0.44/10.66 = 4.1%. The table is internally consistent, and the band ordering (£12.71 > £10.85 > £8.00) holds.

AGE-BAND STRUCTURE CONFIRMED FOR APRIL 2026
The 2026 amendment instrument does not alter the band boundaries. From 1 April 2026 the bands are: 21 and over (National Living Wage); 18 or over but not yet 21; under 18; apprentice. The 21+ threshold and the 18–20 band are therefore as assumed, notwithstanding the historical reductions in the NLW age threshold (25 → 23 → 21).

QUALIFICATIONS A READER SHOULD CARRY
- Statutory vs voluntary: these are the government's statutory National Living Wage / National Minimum Wage. They are not the Living Wage Foundation's voluntary 'real Living Wage' (which is set independently, is higher, and has a separate London figure). The two must not be conflated in contracts, job adverts or payroll specifications.
- No regional variation: NMW/NLW rates are uniform across the UK; there is no separate London statutory rate.
- No transitional rules: NMW/NLW upratings take effect cleanly on 1 April 2026 with no phasing or preservation of the prior rate for existing workers. Payroll periods that straddle 1 April 2026 must apply the new rate to hours worked on or after that date.
- Apprentice and under-18 rates are listed above for completeness but are outside the two requested figures.
- Date of validity: this answer is valid for the rate year beginning 1 April 2026 and is superseded by the next annual uprating (expected 1 April 2027).

SOURCES
- The National Minimum Wage (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/357), legislation.gov.uk — enactment and commencement.
- GOV.UK, 'Minimum wage rates for 2026' — rate table and increases.
- GOV.UK, 'National Minimum Wage rates' — band-by-band April 2026 table.
- GOV.UK, 'The National Minimum Wage in 2026' — Low Pay Commission context.
No authoritative disagreement was found across these sources; the legislation and the GOV.UK rate pages agree on both requested figures and on the band structure.

question: M11
answer:
Compliance determination — FMCSA short-haul exception from records of duty status (RODS).

Governing provision: 49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1), the '150 air-mile radius driver' exception. The rule exempts a driver from the RODS requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if the stated conditions are met.

Answers to the two asks:
1. Radius around the normal work reporting location: 150 air miles. The regulation parenthetically equates this to 172.6 statute miles. The measurement is air miles — straight-line distance — not route miles or kilometers.
2. Consecutive hours within which the driver must be released from work: 14 consecutive hours. The driver, except a driver-salesperson, must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

Quoted regulatory text (49 CFR § 395.1(e)(1)):
'(1) 150 air-mile radius driver. A driver is exempt from the requirements of §§ 395.8 and 395.11 if:
(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;'

Operational meaning for compliance:
- The compliance test for the radius is the straight-line distance from the normal work reporting location to the farthest point the driver operates. Because straight-line distance is never greater than road distance, a trip whose road route is 150 miles or less is necessarily within the radius; a trip whose road route exceeds 150 miles may still be within the radius if the straight-line distance is 150 air miles or less. Do not use route miles, odometer miles, or kilometers as the controlling measure.
- The 14-hour limit is a release-from-work limit, not merely a driving limit. The driver must return to the work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours. The driver may not drive after the 14th hour after coming on duty.
- Other conditions in the same exception continue to apply, including at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each 14-hour on-duty period and the carrier's obligation to maintain accurate time records showing when the driver reports for duty, total hours on duty each day, and when the driver is released from duty.

Provision boundary — avoid conflation:
- The 100 air-mile / 12-hour rule is a separate exception in § 395.1(e)(2) for certain non-CDL drivers. It is not the 150 air-mile short-haul exception and is not the basis for the values stated here. If a non-CDL operation is relying on § 395.1(e)(2), the applicable limits would be 100 air miles and 12 consecutive hours, but that is a different provision.
- The agricultural exceptions and the 150 air-mile non-CDL agricultural variant have their own conditions and should not be substituted for this short-haul determination.

Bottom line: For the FMCSA short-haul exception from RODS, the driver must operate within 150 air miles of the normal work reporting location and must be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED AIRCRAFT LIMITS — CURRENT (IN-FORCE) VALUES

1) Maximum takeoff weight: 12,500 lb — maximum certificated takeoff weight (MCTOW), not the actual takeoff/ramp weight of a given flight.
2) Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry: 7 — including any required flight crewmembers.
3) Passengers on board: 6 — the operational cap on persons carried who are not required flight crewmembers.

All three must be satisfied simultaneously; they are cumulative conditions, not alternatives.

---

OPERATIVE LEGAL TEXT

Authority: 14 CFR 61.113(i) (BasicMed operating limitations), read with 14 CFR 61.23(c)(3) (medical-eligibility pathway) and 14 CFR 68.1–68.11 (BasicMed course/acknowledgment and comprehensive medical examination). Amended by the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Pub. L. 118-63), § 362, and implemented by the FAA final rule published in the Federal Register on 18 November 2024 (FR Doc. 2024-26935), which states that a covered aircraft "may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board."

The statutory basis is commonly cited in FAA BasicMed materials as 49 U.S.C. § 44807 (originally § 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, Pub. L. 114-190). Because the binding, enforceable text is the CFR section, cite 14 CFR 61.113(i) as the controlling source and treat the USC citation as context; confirm the current codification against the eCFR/USC text in force on the date of use.

Element-by-element reading:

- "Maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds." This is a property of the aircraft (its type certificate / airworthiness certificate / approved flight manual limit), not of the flight. An aircraft whose MCTOW is 12,500 lb is inside the limit; one at 12,501 lb is outside, even if it departs at 11,000 lb actual weight. Do not substitute ramp weight, zero-fuel weight, or a pilot-computed actual takeoff weight for MCTOW.
- "Authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers)." This is a certification/authorization limit — the maximum occupancy the aircraft is certificated/configured to carry, with required crew counted inside the 7, not on top of it. An aircraft certificated for 8 or more occupants is not a covered aircraft for BasicMed purposes, regardless of how many seats are filled on the day.
- "Operating with up to 6 passengers on board." This is the in-flight count: persons on board who are not required flight crewmembers. This is the limit a passenger count is checked against at the aircraft door.

---

OCCUPANTS vs. PASSENGERS — RECONCILIATION

The two numbers differ by exactly the required flight crew, which is why 7 and 6 are not in conflict:

  occupants authorized (7) − required flight crewmembers (1) = passengers allowed (6)

The 6-passenger operating cap is an independent ceiling and is not increased if fewer crew are required — 6 is the maximum in every case. Where an operation requires two flight crewmembers, the arithmetic yields 7 − 2 = 5 passengers, i.e., the lower of (occupants authorized − required crew) and 6.

Worked checks (each satisfies all three limits simultaneously):

| Aircraft (example) | MCTOW | Max certificated occupants | Required crew | Passengers allowed | Inside BasicMed? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Four-seat single, e.g. Cessna 172 class | ~2,550 lb | 4 | 1 | min(4−1, 6) = 3 | Yes |
| Six-seat single, e.g. Beech A36 class | ~3,650 lb | 6 | 1 | min(6−1, 6) = 5 | Yes |
| Seven-seat single/twin below 12,500 lb | ≤ 12,500 lb | 7 | 1 | min(7−1, 6) = 6 | Yes |
| Seven-seat aircraft requiring two pilots | ≤ 12,500 lb | 7 | 2 | min(7−2, 6) = 5 | Yes |
| Eight-seat aircraft, 11,000 lb | 11,000 lb | 8 | 1 | n/a — aircraft not eligible | No (occupant authorization exceeds 7) |
| Aircraft at 13,200 lb MCTOW, 6 seats | 13,200 lb | 6 | 1 | n/a — aircraft not eligible | No (MCTOW exceeds 12,500 lb) |

Note the last two rows: eligibility fails on the aircraft's certificated/authorized characteristics even when the day's actual passenger load would have been legal. This is the practical trap — checking seats filled instead of seats authorized, and actual weight instead of MCTOW.

---

SUPERSEDED (PRE-AMENDMENT) FIGURES — DO NOT APPLY

Older FAA material still posted on faa.gov (including AC 68-1A and the 2017-era BasicMed FAQ/newsletter) states the limits as they stood at program inception:

  6,000 lb maximum certificated takeoff weight / 6 occupants / 5 passengers.

These are superseded and must not be used for a current determination. They remain useful only for (a) flights conducted before the amendment took effect, and (b) recognizing stale guidance. Source-currency test: any BasicMed document that pairs 6,000 lb with 6 occupants and 5 passengers predates the 2024 amendment; documents pairing 12,500 lb with 7 occupants and 6 passengers are current. Because the FAA retains both on its site, treat the pair as source-specific, not contradictory, and cite the current Federal Register rule and the current eCFR text of 14 CFR 61.113(i) rather than a cached FAQ PDF.

Note that the superseded set is strictly smaller on all three axes (6,000 < 12,500; 6 < 7; 5 < 6), so no historical value can be mistaken for a current one without violating one of the current ceilings.

---

CONTEXT NOT ASKED BUT EASILY CONFUSED WITH THE LIMITS

The three figures above are aircraft-operating limits. They are separate from, and additional to, the pilot-eligibility conditions for BasicMed: holding a valid U.S. driver's license and a current FAA medical certificate (the most recent of which was not denied, suspended, revoked, or withdrawn), completion of the BasicMed medical education course, a comprehensive medical examination within the preceding 48 months, the required physician-signed checklist, and operating under the self-certification/acknowledgment framework of 14 CFR part 68. A pilot who meets every aircraft limit above but fails an eligibility condition may not operate under BasicMed. Do not fold these conditions into the aircraft figures, and do not present the aircraft figures as a complete statement of BasicMed authority.

---

VERIFICATION CHECKLIST (run before relying on the answer)

1. Confirm 12,500 / 7 / 6 against the eCFR text of 14 CFR 61.113(i) in force on the date of use — the CFR, not a PDF FAQ, is controlling.
2. Confirm the aircraft's MCTOW from its type certificate data sheet, airworthiness certificate, or approved flight manual — not from a loading calculation.
3. Confirm the aircraft's maximum certificated/authorized occupancy (seat count with required crew counted inside the total) is ≤ 7.
4. Count bodies at the door: required flight crewmembers are excluded from the passenger count, and that count must be ≤ 6.
5. Reject any guidance pairing 6,000 lb / 6 occupants / 5 passengers as current.

---

SOURCES

- 14 CFR 61.113(i) (current eCFR text) — controlling regulation.
- FAA final rule, FR Doc. 2024-26935, Federal Register, 18 November 2024 — https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2024-11-18/html/2024-26935.htm (quoted: "A covered aircraft may now be authorized to carry up to 7 occupants (including any required flight crewmembers) and may be operating with up to 6 passengers on board.")
- FAA BasicMed program page — https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med
- FAA newsroom, "FAA Updates BasicMed Program" — https://www.faa.gov/newsroom/faa-updates-basicmed-program
- FAA BasicMed FAQ (current edition) — https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med/basicmed_faq.pdf
- AC 68-1A — https://www.faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_68-1a.pdf (contains superseded 6,000 lb / 6 occupant / 5 passenger figures; use for historical context only)
- FAA BasicMed newsletter, Jul/Aug 2017 — https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med/JulAug2017.pdf (historical; superseded)
- FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Pub. L. 118-63, § 362 — statutory amendment.
