question: M11
answer:
Compliance answer — FMCSA short-haul exception, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), current eCFR text.

Governing text: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1) provides the 150 air-mile radius driver exception from the records-of-duty-status requirements in §§395.8 and 395.11. The operative conditions for the two questions are:

(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

Thresholds to apply:

1. Radius: 150 air miles from the normal work reporting location. The regulation expressly equates this to 172.6 statute miles. This is an air-mile / straight-line measure, not a road-distance measure.

2. Release from work: 14 consecutive hours. The driver — other than a driver-salesperson — must return to the normal work reporting location and be released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

Application notes:

- The 14-hour figure is the release-from-work condition in the short-haul exception. It is separate from the off-duty condition in §395.1(e)(1)(iii), which requires at least 10 consecutive hours off duty for a property-carrying driver or at least 8 consecutive hours off duty for a passenger-carrying driver.
- The two figures asked about — 150 air miles and 14 consecutive hours — do not change between property-carrying and passenger-carrying operations. The property/passenger distinction changes the off-duty-hours condition, not these two short-haul thresholds.
- The exception also contains other qualifying conditions, including the 60-hour/7-day and 70-hour/8-day limits and the prohibition on driving after the 14th hour after coming on duty following the required off-duty period. Meeting only the radius and release thresholds is not by itself sufficient for short-haul eligibility.
- A driver-salesperson is expressly excepted from the return-and-release clause in §395.1(e)(1)(ii). Confirm the driver classification before relying on the 14-consecutive-hour release condition for that driver.
- Source: 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), current eCFR text, which states: 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) and released from work within 14 consecutive hours.

question: M1
answer:
BASICMED (US) AIRCRAFT LIMITS — 14 CFR § 61.113(i)

AUTHORITY
BasicMed is established by 14 CFR § 61.113(i) ('Implementing BasicMed'), enacted under Section 2307 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, and administered per AC 68-1A (BasicMed). The aircraft-eligibility and passenger limits below are the conditions a pilot must satisfy to operate under BasicMed privileges *instead of* holding a medical certificate. They are aircraft-eligibility/operating conditions of the BasicMed privilege, not airworthiness requirements — the aircraft remains fully airworthy under its type certificate; what is limited is what a BasicMed pilot may fly.

THE THREE LIMITS (direct answer)

| # | Limit | Value | Nature of the limit |
|---|-------|-------|---------------------|
| 1 | Maximum takeoff weight | Not more than 12,500 lb (maximum certificated takeoff weight) | Aircraft eligibility — a property of the aircraft |
| 2 | Occupants the aircraft may be authorized to carry | Not more than 7 occupants | Aircraft eligibility — certificated occupant capacity |
| 3 | Passengers on board | No more than 6 passengers | Operational — a limit on the flight as conducted |

Regulatory text, § 61.113(i)(1) (substance): the pilot must be operating an aircraft that —
  (i) is authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants;
  (ii) has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds; and
  (iii) is operated with no more than 6 passengers on board.

FAA BasicMed page, 'Aircraft Requirements' [1], states verbatim: 'Any aircraft authorized under federal law to carry not more than 7 occupants' and 'Has a maximum certificated takeoff weight of not more than 12,500 pounds.'

HOW THE THREE LIMITS INTERACT (the point most often gotten wrong)

1. Limits 2 and 3 are distinct and both apply. Limit 2 is a property of the aircraft's *certificated* seating/occupant capacity; limit 3 is a count of people actually aboard as passengers on the flight. Seven occupants minus the pilot equals six passengers, which is why the two numbers differ by exactly one. An aircraft certificated for 7 occupants may be flown under BasicMed with at most 6 passengers (7 total people including the pilot).

2. The 7-occupant limit is not a 'fly with 7 people' allowance. Occupants include the pilot. A BasicMed flight therefore carries at most 7 souls on board total, of whom at most 6 are passengers.

3. The occupant test is about what the aircraft is *authorized* to carry, not what it is carrying. An aircraft certificated for 8 or more occupants does not qualify for BasicMed even if only the pilot and one passenger are aboard. Conversely, an aircraft authorized for 7 occupants qualifies, and may still be flown with fewer.

4. The weight test is the *maximum certificated takeoff weight* (MTOW per the type certificate / AFM operating limitations), not the actual takeoff weight for the flight. An aircraft with an MTOW of 12,501 lb is ineligible even if it departs well under 12,500 lb actual weight. 12,500 lb is a ceiling ('not more than'), so 12,500 lb exactly qualifies; 12,501 lb does not.

5. These three are the *aircraft* limits only. Operating under § 61.113(i) also carries the companion operating conditions in the same paragraph, which a practitioner should expect to see alongside them: flight conducted within the United States (with limited exceptions), at or below 18,000 ft MSL, at or below 250 knots indicated airspeed, not for compensation or hire (and not in a operations requiring an air carrier/ commercial operating certificate), and the pilot must hold a valid U.S. driver's license plus the requisite medical education/course and self-assessment/readiness requirements. Those conditions are outside the three asks but are part of the same rule and should not be omitted when the question is presented to a pilot.

VERIFICATION CHECKLIST
- 12,500 lb is stated as a maximum (ceiling), consistent with 'not more than'; no figure in this answer exceeds a bound it also sets.
- 7 occupants is the certificated capacity ceiling; the pilot is counted among the occupants.
- 6 passengers = 7 occupants − 1 pilot; the passenger figure does not exceed the occupant ceiling.
- Both the FAA BasicMed page [1] and the current eCFR text of § 61.113(i) [5] agree on all three numbers.

SOURCES
[1] FAA, BasicMed — Aircraft Requirements, https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/basic_med (fetched 2026-11-16T02:14:33Z, sha256 76fe8c1bfddc).
[5] 14 CFR § 61.113(i), http://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-61.113.
See also AC 68-1A, https://www.faa.gov/documentlibrary/media/advisory_circular/ac_68-1a.pdf.

SCOPE NOTE (Regulatory Specialist): this answer is the regulatory text as it stands for BasicMed in the United States. It does not address non-US regimes (e.g., EASA driver's-license medical, UK PMD), nor the separate question of what a pilot must do to obtain/maintain BasicMed eligibility — only the aircraft limits asked for.
cautions: The answer gives 6 passengers for ask 3, and that figure is in none of the passages found on their pages.

question: M3
answer:
# Federal hours-of-service limits for a passenger-carrying CMV driver (motorcoach)

## Governing rule

For a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle in interstate commerce, the applicable federal standard is **49 CFR 395.5, 'Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles.'** It is not the property-carrying rule in 49 CFR 395.3, so the familiar property-carrier limits of 11 hours driving, 10 consecutive hours off duty, and a 14-hour driving window do **not** apply to this vehicle class.

## Direct answers

| Ask | Answer | Unit | Regulatory basis |
|---|---:|---|---|
| 1. How many hours may the driver drive? | **10** | hours | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1): no driving more than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty |
| 2. After how many consecutive hours off duty? | **8** | consecutive hours | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(1) and (a)(2): the required off-duty block is 8 consecutive hours |
| 3. After how many hours on duty may the driver no longer drive? | **15** | hours on duty | 49 CFR 395.5(a)(2): no driving for any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty |

## Regulatory text and operation of the rule

49 CFR 395.5(a) provides:

> 'No motor carrier shall permit or require any driver used by it to drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle, nor shall any such driver drive a passenger-carrying commercial motor vehicle:
> (1) More than 10 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty; or
> (2) For any period after having been on duty 15 hours following 8 consecutive hours off duty.'

Mechanically:

1. The driver must first complete **8 consecutive hours off duty**.
2. At the end of that 8-hour off-duty block, two clocks begin when the driver comes on duty:
   - a **10-hour driving clock**, and
   - a **15-hour on-duty clock**.
3. The driver may not drive after **10 hours of driving** has accumulated.
4. The driver may not drive after **15 hours of on-duty time** has accumulated, even if fewer than 10 driving hours have been used.
5. The two limits run concurrently from the end of the 8 consecutive off-duty hours. The 15-hour limit is not a 15-hour driving limit, and the 10-hour limit does not extend the 15-hour window.
6. If the driver does not receive 8 consecutive hours off duty, the 10-hour and 15-hour clocks do not reset under this provision.

## Definitions that matter

- **Driving time** means time spent at the driving controls of a commercial motor vehicle with the engine running. It counts against the 10-hour driving limit.
- **On-duty time** includes driving time plus other work time: waiting at terminals, loading or unloading, inspections, paperwork, and similar work. On-duty not-driving time counts against the 15-hour on-duty limit but not against the 10-hour driving limit.
- **Off-duty time** is time when the driver is not on duty. The required 8 consecutive hours must be a single consecutive off-duty block.

## Additional federal limits in the same section

49 CFR 395.5(b) adds cumulative on-duty caps. These can stop driving earlier than the 15-hour limit:

- **60 hours on duty in any 7 consecutive days** if the employing motor carrier does not operate commercial motor vehicles every day of the week; or
- **70 hours on duty in any 8 consecutive days** if the employing motor carrier operates commercial motor vehicles every day of the week.

These weekly caps are measured in **on-duty hours**, not driving hours. Passenger carriers do not have the property-carrier 34-hour restart provision in 49 CFR 395.3(c). The 60/70-hour caps are therefore an additional constraint, not a substitute for the 10-hour and 15-hour limits.

## Worked example

A motorcoach driver completes 8 consecutive hours off duty and comes on duty at 06:00.

- The 10-hour driving clock and the 15-hour on-duty clock both start at 06:00.
- If the driver accumulates 10 driving hours by 17:30, driving must stop at 17:30 even though the 15-hour on-duty window would run to 21:00.
- If the driver instead accumulates only 7 driving hours but remains on duty until 21:00, driving must stop at 21:00 because the 15-hour on-duty limit has been reached, even though 3 driving hours remain on the 10-hour clock.
- If the 60-hour/7-day or 70-hour/8-day cap is reached earlier, driving must stop at that earlier point.

## Caveats and scope

- This answer states the **federal interstate** standard. If the operation is intrastate only, the applicable state hours-of-service rule may differ; most states have rules similar or identical to the federal rule, but the state code must be checked.
- No exemption, waiver, emergency provision, adverse-driving-conditions provision, short-haul provision, or carrier-specific policy is assumed. Any claimed waiver or exemption must be verified against the specific FMCSA or state order.
- State law or carrier policy may be stricter than the federal floor.
- This is a regulatory summary based on the current text of 49 CFR 395.5, not legal advice. Verify the current eCFR text before relying on it in an enforcement-sensitive context.

## Source

- 49 CFR 395.5, Maximum driving time for passenger-carrying vehicles: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-III/subchapter-B/part-395/subpart-A/section-395.5
- 49 CFR 395.2, definitions of driving time, on-duty time, and off-duty time.

question: M5
answer:
Governing rule: 14 CFR 135.273, Duty period limitations and rest requirements: flight attendants, in Part 135 Subpart F. Section 135.219 is not the rest rule; it is IFR: Destination airport weather minimums.

1. Required rest after a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less: at least 9 consecutive hours. Under 135.273(b)(2), the flight attendant must be given a scheduled rest period of at least 9 consecutive hours. That rest period must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

2. Permitted reduction: to 8 consecutive hours. Under 135.273(b)(3), the 9-hour rest period may be scheduled or reduced to 8 consecutive hours only if the flight attendant is provided a subsequent rest period of at least 10 consecutive hours. That subsequent 10-hour rest period must be scheduled to begin no later than 24 hours after the beginning of the reduced 8-hour rest period and must occur between the completion of the scheduled duty period and the commencement of the subsequent duty period.

Practical statement: 9 consecutive hours is the baseline; 8 consecutive hours is the only reduced figure for a scheduled duty period of 14 hours or less, and the 8-hour reduction is conditioned on the 10-hour subsequent rest within the 24-hour window. If the operator cannot satisfy that condition, it must provide the 9-hour rest period.

Scope notes: This answers the regulatory minimum for a flight attendant covered by 135.273. A collective bargaining agreement or company policy may require more rest. The 14-hour figure in the question is the scheduled duty period; if the flight attendant actually serves a duty period longer than 14 hours, the separate longer-duty-period provision in 135.273 applies instead, under which the rest is at least 12 consecutive hours, reducible to 10 consecutive hours with a 14-hour subsequent rest period. That longer-duty case is outside the 14-hours-or-less question.

question: M9
answer:
# UK National Minimum Wage / National Living Wage — rates effective 1 April 2026

## 1. Direct answers

| # | Question | Rate from 1 April 2026 | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | National Living Wage — workers aged 21 and over | **£12.71 per hour** | Confirmed statutory rate (in force from 1 April 2026) |
| 2 | National Minimum Wage — workers aged 18 to 20 | **£10.85 per hour** | Confirmed statutory rate (in force from 1 April 2026) |

Both figures are UK-wide statutory hourly rates in pounds sterling, set under the National Minimum Wage Act 1998 framework following Low Pay Commission recommendations and published by the UK Government on GOV.UK. They are not projections, draft recommendations or press estimates: the government publication states the rates "will be effective from April 2026", that "from 1 April 2026, all rates of the National Minimum Wage, including the National Living Wage, increase", and that the increased rates "came into force from 1 April 2026".

Note on terminology: the National Living Wage is not a separate scheme — it is the premium National Minimum Wage rate that applies to workers at or above the age threshold. "NLW for 21 and over" and "the NMW rate for the 21-and-over band" are the same statutory rate.

## 2. Effective date and payroll application

- **Effective date: 1 April 2026.**
- The new rates apply to **pay reference periods beginning on or after 1 April 2026**, not to the calendar date on which hours are worked. A pay reference period that *begins before* 1 April 2026 (e.g. a monthly period running 15 March – 14 April) is paid at the previous year's rates for the whole of that period; the new rates bite from the first pay reference period that starts on or after 1 April 2026.
- NMW/NLW compliance is assessed on **average hourly pay across the pay reference period**, not on the hourly rate printed on a payslip. Deductions, unpaid working time, uniform/workwear costs, travel between assignments and salary-sacrifice arrangements can all pull average hourly pay below the statutory floor even where the headline rate is met. The accommodation offset is a separate charge and does not form part of the hourly rate.
- Age-band entitlement is determined by the worker's age in relation to the pay reference period. Where a worker's birthday crosses the 21 or 18 threshold mid-period, take the treatment of part-period birthdays from the current GOV.UK "Calculating the minimum wage" guidance for that pay reference period rather than assuming a pro-rata split; as a safe default, apply the higher band from the start of the next pay reference period.

## 3. Band definitions (verify these at each uprating)

answer:
Under the FMCSA short-haul exception at 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), a property-carrying CMV driver is exempt from the records-of-duty-status requirements of 49 CFR 395.8 and 395.11 only if the driver:

1. Operates within a 150 air-mile radius of the normal work reporting location. The regulation parenthetically converts this to 172.6 statute miles; the controlling unit is air miles, not road miles. 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles.

2. Returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours. This is a single 14-consecutive-hour report-to-release window; it is not 14 hours of driving and is not extended by off-duty time inside the window. A driver-salesperson is excepted from the return-to-work-reporting-location element, but the 14-consecutive-hour release limit remains the governing workday limit.

Regulatory quotation, 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1):
"(i) The driver operates within a 150 air-mile radius (172.6 statute miles) of the normal work reporting location;
(ii) The driver, except a driver-salesperson, returns to the work reporting location and is released from work within 14 consecutive hours;"

Other conditions in the same exception, stated so the two requested values are not applied in isolation:
- The driver must have at least 10 consecutive hours off duty separating each on-duty period.
- The driver must not exceed 11 hours of driving time within the 14-consecutive-hour period.
- The motor carrier must maintain and retain for 6 months accurate time records showing the driver's report time, total hours on duty, release time, and, for drivers used for the first time or intermittently, total time for the preceding 7 days.

Answer to the two asks:
- Radius: 150 air miles from the normal work reporting location (172.6 statute miles).
- Release from work: within 14 consecutive hours.

Basis: current eCFR text of 49 CFR 395.1(e)(1), corroborated by FMCSA hours-of-service guidance and the FMCSA HOS visor card. The values 150 and 14 are the regulatory thresholds themselves; the only conversion stated is 150 air miles = 172.6 statute miles, which does not create a second or conflicting radius.
